h:nigella.x:
Black seed (nigella) Nigella sativa
See real photos of the plant ↗
Other names الحبة السوداء، الشونيز، السانوج، القزحة · Black seed Part used Seeds, oil Strength of evidence Moderate
For children The seeds on bread and food only, not the oil.
Blood sugar & lipids Blood pressure Colds & cough Postpartum Breastfeeding Seasonal allergies Cholesterol Easy to grow at home
In Islamic heritage
Authentic (sahih) hadith The Prophet ﷺ said: “In the black seed is healing for every disease except death” (Bukhari and Muslim).
Extended guide
Its forms
Whole seeds: lightly toasted and ground when used; they keep longer.
Powder: loses its aromatic oil quickly, so grind small amounts.
Oil: cold-pressed, with a sharp smell and pungent taste; the form most used in studies.
Capsules: oil in a fixed dose; the most accurate amount.
In the Sunnah and scholars' understanding
The Prophet ﷺ said: “In the black seed is healing for every disease except death” (Bukhari and Muslim).
Many commentators on the hadith held that «every disease» is a general phrase with a specific meaning — that it benefits many illnesses that can be treated with it, not that it replaces every treatment. Treating with it does not conflict with using medicine, for the Prophet ﷺ said: “Seek treatment, servants of God.”
What does the science say?
Moderate A slight drop in mildly raised blood pressure.
Moderate A slight drop in bad cholesterol and triglycerides.
Moderate A slight improvement in blood sugar in type 2 diabetes, alongside medicine, not instead of it.
Limited Nasal allergy and mild asthma.
Limited A helper in treating stomach H. pylori alongside medical treatment.
Not true Treating cancer: the studies are lab-only, with no evidence in humans.
Amounts used in studies
Ground seeds: 1–3 grams daily (about half to one teaspoon).
Oil: 500 mg to 1 g capsules twice daily.
Usually for 8–12 weeks, then assess the benefit.
Safety
Its oil on the skin may cause allergic inflammation and blisters: test on a small area first.
It may lower blood sugar and blood pressure, so monitor readings with their medicines.
It may slightly increase bleeding: caution with blood thinners, and stop two weeks before surgery.
Rare cases of kidney damage with large doses have been recorded: do not exceed the usual amounts.
Pregnant and breastfeeding women: food amounts only.
Buying and storage
Good oil is cold-pressed, in a dark bottle, with a strong, sharp smell.
Keep away from light and heat, and use within months of opening.
Good seeds are glossy black and release their scent when rubbed.
Common uses
Support for blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol (slight drops in small trials)
Nasal allergy and mild asthma symptoms (limited evidence)
An everyday addition to bread and food
Usual preparation
The seeds are eaten roasted and ground with honey, or sprinkled on food.
Cautions
The oil on the skin may cause allergic dermatitis
Pregnancy: food amounts only
Possible drug interactions
Diabetes and blood-pressure medicines (added effect)
Blood thinners
Sedatives
Growing and propagation
Easy in the Gulf

h:frankincense.x:
Frankincense (kundur, Dhofar frankincense) Boswellia sacra / serrata
See real photos of the plant ↗
Other names الكندر، لبان ظفار، اللبان الذكر · Frankincense Part used Resin Strength of evidence Moderate
For children Not recommended for children except as prescribed by a doctor.
Pain & inflammation Mouth & throat Digestion & bloating
Extended guide
Types of frankincense
Kind The tree and where it grows Features
Omani (Dhofari) Boswellia sacra , Dhofar in Oman, and Mahra and Hadramawt in Yemen The finest is «Hojari», followed by Najdi, Shazri and Shaabi. Greenish-white to yellow tears with a lemony scent
Somali Boswellia sacra / carteri , northern Somalia Common in Gulf markets, and similar to the Omani
Maydi Boswellia frereana , northern Somalia Chewed like gum, and it lacks the boswellic acids studied for joints
Ethiopian, Eritrean and Sudanese Boswellia papyrifera , Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan Cheaper, and used more for incense
Indian Boswellia serrata , India Most of the studied joint supplements come from it
«Kundur» is its name in old medical books, and «male frankincense» means the good round tears. In Egypt, «luban» means chewing gum.
History
The incense route: Caravans carried it from Dhofar and Hadramawt north across Arabia to Gaza and the Mediterranean ports, enriching the kingdoms of Saba, Hadramawt, Ma'in and Qataban, and later the Nabataeans.
«The Land of Frankincense»: UNESCO inscribed it as World Heritage in 2000. It includes the trees of Wadi Dawkah, the oasis of Shisr (Wubar), and the ports of Khor Rori (Sumhuram) and Al-Baleed in Dhofar.
Ancient Egypt: Queen Hatshepsut sent an expedition to the land of «Punt» that returned with frankincense trees, and the journey was carved on the walls of her temple at Deir el-Bahari.
Arab medicine: Ibn Sina mentioned it as kundur for cough and the stomach, and it was famous among them for strengthening memory.
In the hadith: No specific authentic hadith exists about frankincense. Ibn al-Qayyim said the hadith «Fumigate your homes with frankincense and wormwood» is not authentic, and the story circulated about burning frankincense in Madinah during a plague has no basis.
Gulf customs
Chewing: A small tear chewed like gum to freshen the mouth.
Frankincense water: Tears soaked overnight, and the water drunk for the stomach.
Fumigation: In homes, majlis gatherings, at Eid and when welcoming guests.
Fumigating water jars: An old Omani custom of perfuming the clay jar with smoke before filling it, to sweeten the taste of the water.
What does the science say?
Moderate Knee osteoarthritis: A 2020 review of 7 trials with 545 patients found that boswellia extract eased pain and stiffness and improved movement, when taken for at least 4 weeks. Most of these trials used standardised extracts of the Indian type, not soaked frankincense.
Limited Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis and Crohn's): Small, conflicting trials, and a larger trial in Crohn's disease found no difference from placebo.
Limited Asthma: Few small trials.
Limited Memory: Despite its fame in heritage, most studies are in animals.
Limited Cancer: Laboratory results only, and frankincense is not a cancer treatment.
Soaked frankincense water has hardly been studied, and the active substances in frankincense dissolve poorly in water.
Incense and the lungs
In a 2009 Omani study of 2441 children, burning incense more than twice a week was linked to children's breathing being affected, and incense triggered wheezing in about 38% of children with asthma. It was not linked to more children developing asthma itself.
Burn incense in an open space or with good ventilation.
No incense in the room of a baby or of someone with asthma or allergy.
Burning charcoal releases carbon monoxide, so do not leave it lit in a closed room where people sleep.
Amount and use
Frankincense water: 5 to 6 small tears soaked in a cup of water overnight.
Chewing: One small pure tear, not swallowed.
Joint supplements: A standardised extract from a trusted source at the dose on the package; in studies, 100 mg to 1 gram a day depending on the type of extract.
Safety
It may cause stomach upset or heartburn.
The essential oil is not to be swallowed, and is diluted before putting it on the skin, as it may cause allergy.
With medicines: Consult a doctor if you take blood thinners or anti-inflammatory painkillers.
Pregnancy: Avoid extracts. Frankincense water is common but its safety in pregnancy has not been studied, so keep to moderation and ask your doctor.
Children: Do not give frankincense tears to young children because of the risk of choking.
Common myths
«Frankincense water in pregnancy makes the baby intelligent»: There is no evidence for this, and its safety in pregnancy has not been studied.
«Frankincense oil cures cancer»: Laboratory results only, and leaving treatment for it is dangerous.
«Frankincense strengthens students' memory»: An old tradition, and the evidence in humans is weak.

Black-seed honey Black-seed farms Dark, with a strong distinctive smell
There is not enough evidence to prefer one kind over another for home use, except sterile medical honey for treating wounds.
What does the science say?
Relatively strong Night-time cough in children over one and adults; some British medical guidelines recommend trying it for acute cough.
Moderate Superficial wounds and burns with sterile medical honey (not kitchen honey).
Moderate Mouth inflammation from radiotherapy, after asking the treating team.
Limited Small mouth ulcers and an irritated throat.
Not true Weight loss and treating diabetes: honey is a natural sugar that raises blood sugar.
Common myths
«Crystallised honey is fake»: not true; crystallisation is natural and happens faster in clover honey and in the cold. Warm it in a water bath to make it liquid again.
«The thumb, water or lighter test reveals fake honey»: these tests are unreliable; laboratory testing is what decides.
«Heating honey turns it into poison»: not true; strong, long heating loses some enzymes and flavour, but adding it to a warm drink is safe. It is best added once the drink is lukewarm.
«Honey never goes off»: good honey keeps a very long time, but moisture makes it ferment.
Storage
In a tightly closed glass jar at room temperature, away from the sun.
Do not keep it in the fridge, as cold speeds up crystallisation.
Always use a clean, dry spoon so no moisture gets in.
Important warnings
Completely forbidden under one year of age in any form, even on a dummy, because of the risk of botulism.
Diabetics count it as part of their sugars.
«Mad honey» from rhododendron flowers in Turkey and Nepal is poisonous and causes a fall in blood pressure and pulse.
People allergic to bees or pollen should be careful with raw honey and propolis.
Kitchen honey must not be put on open wounds; only sterile medical honey.

Verse of the Quran The Prophet ﷺ said: «Whoever eats seven ajwa dates every morning will not be harmed that day by poison or magic» (Bukhari and Muslim). And God said to Mary: «Shake the trunk of the palm tree towards you; it will drop fresh ripe dates upon you» [Maryam: 25]. And the Prophet ﷺ was eating palm heart (jummar) when he said: «Among the trees is a tree that is like the Muslim… it is the palm tree» (Bukhari and Muslim).
Extended guide
Famous varieties
Variety Origin Features
Ajwa Madinah Small, dark and soft; mentioned in the hadith
Sukkari Qassim Golden, very sweet, sometimes crisp
Khalas Al-Ahsa Amber; among the finest dates of the Gulf
Barhi Iraq and the Gulf Eaten as crunchy yellow khalal or as fresh rutab
Medjool Morocco, Palestine and Jordan Large, soft and fleshy
Deglet Nour Tunisia and Algeria Translucent honey colour, semi-dry
Sagai, Safawi and Khudri Najd and Madinah Common everyday varieties of varying sweetness
Khenaizi and Lulu The Gulf and the UAE Dark and soft, medium sweetness
Zahdi and Braim Iraq Semi-dry; date syrup (dibs) is made from it
Stages of ripening
Tal': the first growth from the palm.
Balah or khalal: green then yellow or red, with an astringent taste.
Busr: full colour, sweetness beginning.
Rutab: soft and juicy, with more water and less sugar per date.
Tamr: dried, with concentrated sugar; keeps for a long time.
In the Quran and Sunnah
God said to Maryam during labour: “Shake the trunk of the palm tree toward you; it will drop on you ripe, fresh dates” [Quran 19:25].
«Whoever eats seven ajwa dates every morning will not be harmed that day by poison or magic” (Bukhari and Muslim).
«A house without dates — its people are hungry” (Muslim).
The Prophet ﷺ used to break his fast with fresh dates; if there were none, then dried dates; if there were none, he took a few sips of water (Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi).
The Prophet ﷺ used to do tahnik for newborns with a date (Bukhari and Muslim).
What does the science say?
Relatively strong A food rich in fibre, potassium, magnesium and antioxidants.
Moderate The last weeks of pregnancy: trials and reviews found that eating about 6 dates a day in the last four weeks was linked to better cervical readiness and less need for induction. Ask your doctor, especially with gestational diabetes.
Moderate Constipation, thanks to the fibre.
Moderate Despite their sweetness, many varieties have a moderate glycaemic index, but the amount matters most for diabetics.
The Sunnah of tahnik and the newborn's safety
Tahnik is chewing a little date and rubbing it on the newborn's palate.
Wash the hands well, chew the date until very soft, and rub it on the palate with a very light touch.
Very important: no one with a cold sore (herpes) on the lip or a cold should do tahnik; serious herpes infections in newborns caught from adults' saliva have been recorded.
Do not put pieces of date in a newborn's mouth, and do not give date water or honey to a baby.
For diabetes and kidney patients
Diabetes: two or three dates within the allowance, with protein or healthy fats (yoghurt, nuts) to soften the rise in blood sugar, and measure your sugar afterwards to learn their effect on you.
Advanced kidney disease: dates are rich in potassium, so agree the amount with the doctor.
Storage and buying
Fresh dates (rutab) are kept in the fridge and eaten within days; they can be frozen.
Dried dates in an airtight container in a cool, dry place, or in the fridge for longer.
Avoid dates coated with glucose or shiny syrup.
Date stones are roasted and ground into a caffeine-free «coffee»; data on its benefits are few.

High in sugar: for diabetics, two or three dates within the allowance

Which part is safe?
Leaves: the safest; eaten as a vegetable in India, Africa and the Philippines.
Green pods: cooked in Indian cuisine (sambar).
Seeds and their oil: ban oil for skin, hair and food.
Roots and bark: they contain toxic substances and may cause the womb to contract; do not use them .
What does the science say?
Relatively strong The leaves are a food rich in protein, calcium, iron and vitamin A, useful for nutrition where food is scarce.
Limited Lowering blood sugar and lipids: small studies with inconsistent results.
Limited Increasing breast milk: small encouraging trials.
Limited Anaemia: a plant source of iron, but it does not replace a doctor's treatment.
The claim that it «treats 300 diseases» has no scientific basis.
Usual amount
One to two teaspoons of leaf powder daily in food or warm water. Start with half a teaspoon, as it may cause diarrhoea or an upset stomach at first.
Before buying
Buy from a licensed source; contaminants and heavy metals have been found in some powders.
A bright green colour and a grassy smell are signs of a good powder.
Genuine ban oil is rare and expensive, and often adulterated.

Extended guide
Parts of the sidr tree
Leaves: dried and ground; they contain foaming substances that clean like soap.
Nabq: a small sweet-sour fruit, eaten fresh or dried.
Sidr honey: one of the most famous honeys of Yemen and Saudi Arabia.
The tree: the shade of the desert; its roots withstand drought.
How to prepare a sidr wash
Mix 3 tablespoons of ground sidr leaves with warm water into a paste.
Whisk by hand or with a spoon until it foams.
Spread it on the hair or body and leave for 10–15 minutes, then rinse well.
What does the science say?
Limited Lab studies suggest antifungal and antibacterial properties in sidr leaves.
There are not enough human trials for treating dandruff or hair loss, but it is a gentle cleanser that is safe for most people.
Nabq is a food rich in vitamin C.

It may dry dry hair, so follow with oil.
Keep away from the eyes.
Test on a small area if your skin is sensitive.
The nabq stone is hard: remove it for children to avoid choking.

See real photos of the plant ↗
Other names الحناء · Henna Part used Leaves Strength of evidence Limited
For children Not recommended for children except as prescribed by a doctor.
Hair & scalp Skin & wounds Easy to grow at home
In Islamic heritage
Authentic (sahih) hadith The Prophet ﷺ said: “The best thing with which you change grey hair is henna and katam” (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, Nasa'i and Ibn Majah; graded authentic by Tirmidhi). And no one complained to him ﷺ of pain in the legs without him saying: “Dye them with henna” (Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi; graded good by some scholars).
Extended guide
Pure and adulterated henna
Pure: a greenish-brown powder with a grassy smell; its colour on the skin starts orange, then darkens to reddish-brown within a day or two.
«Black henna»: an instant black colour within minutes. This usually means it contains PPD, which has caused burns, scars and permanent allergy. Avoid it completely.
Ready-made henna cones for designs: some contain chemicals; read the ingredients and buy from a trusted source.
Compound» henna: some contains metal salts that react with chemical salon dyes; do not dye your hair with a chemical dye afterwards without asking a specialist.
Allergy test before use
Put a little paste behind the ear or inside the elbow.
Leave it for an hour, then wash it off.
Watch the spot for 48 hours: if redness, itching or swelling appears, do not use it.
Henna and grey hair
Henna alone gives white hair an orange or copper colour.
For brown or black: apply henna first and rinse, then apply indigo or katam in a second step (see the recipe).
Mixing henna with indigo in different ratios gives shades of brown.
Safety
Do not apply to babies and young children , or to people with G6PD deficiency (favism), which is common in the Gulf; it may cause breakdown of red blood cells and jaundice.
Do not apply to broken or deeply cracked skin.
External use only.
Common uses
Dyeing, strengthening and adding shine to hair
Covering grey hair (with katam or indigo for a darker colour)
Decorating hands and feet
Cracked feet and cooling them (traditional use)
Usual preparation
Mix the leaf powder into a paste with warm water and leave for hours.
Cautions
«Black» henna contains PPD and causes burns and severe allergy: forbidden
Do not apply to babies or to people with G6PD deficiency (may cause breakdown of red blood cells)

h:gumarabic.x:
Gum arabic (hashab) Acacia senegal (Senegalia senegal)
See real photos of the plant ↗
Other names الصمغ، صمغ عربي، الهشاب، صمغ الهشاب، صمغ الطلح، صمغ الأكاسيا، موية الصمغ · Gum arabic Part used The gum (hardened sap of the trunk) Strength of evidence Moderate
For children In food in small amounts only; therapeutic amounts for children only under a doctor's supervision.
Digestion & bloating Constipation Diarrhoea Kidneys
Extended guide
Where does it come from?
Farmers cut the bark of the tree after the rainy season, and sap flows out and hardens in the air into lumps that are collected weeks later. The trees grow in the «gum arabic belt» across the African Sahel from Senegal to Sudan and Eritrea. Before the war that began in 2023, Sudan exported about 70 to 80% of the world's hashab gum, and the finest comes from Kordofan.
Kind The tree and where it grows Features
Hashab Acacia senegal , Sudan, Chad, Nigeria and Senegal The finest type: hard round lumps, from yellowish white to light amber, that dissolve completely in water. Most studies use it
Talh Acacia seyal , Sudan and East Africa Brittle, slightly darker flakes of lower quality, used more in industry
Samr gum Acacia tortilis , Arabian Peninsula and the UAE A local gum from the samr tree; it is not the commercial gum arabic, and there are no medical studies on it
History and heritage
Ancient Egypt: Acacia gum was used to mix paints and inks, and in mummification.
The name: Arab traders carried it from Africa through the ports of the Arabian Peninsula to Europe, so Europeans called it «gum arabic».
Arab medicine: The old Arab physicians mention it for a rough throat, cough and diarrhoea, because it coats the throat and intestines with a slippery layer.
In the Quran: Allah says: ﴿And talh trees layered with fruit﴾ [Al-Waqi'ah: 29]. Some commentators explained talh as the acacia tree known to the Arabs, while others said it is the banana.
In Sudan: «Gum water» (moyat al-samgh) is a home drink soaked overnight and drunk in the morning, and traditionally given to kidney patients.
In politics: When the United States imposed sanctions on Sudan in the 1990s, it exempted gum arabic, because soft drink and confectionery factories needed it.
In your food and medicines without your knowing
It is labelled «E414», «acacia gum» or «Gum arabic», and is used:
In soft drinks and juices, to keep the flavour oil mixed with the water.
In sweets, chewing gum, marshmallows and ice cream.
In tablets as a binder and coating.
In watercolour paints and inks, and it was once the glue on postage stamps.
The European Food Safety Authority reviewed its safety in 2017 and found no cause for concern at food levels.
What does the science say?
Moderate Food for the good gut bacteria: About 85 to 90% of it is soluble fibre that ferments in the colon. In a trial of 54 volunteers (2008), 10 grams a day for 4 weeks increased the good bacteria, and this was the best dose.
Limited Constipation and mild diarrhoea: Soluble fibre regulates the stool, but evidence for gum arabic alone is limited. In severe diarrhoea, oral rehydration solution remains the basis.
Limited Chronic kidney disease: Small trials, mostly in Sudan; a 2022 review found only 4 studies and pointed to lower urea and creatinine. Gut bacteria are thought to use up some urea while fermenting the gum. It does not replace dialysis or medicines.
Limited Sickle cell anaemia: In a Sudanese trial of 47 patients, 30 grams a day for 12 weeks slightly raised fetal haemoglobin (from 6.7% to 7.4%), with no comparison group.
Limited Cholesterol, blood sugar and weight: Few and conflicting results.
Usual amount
In studies: 10 to 30 grams a day dissolved in water.
Start with 1 teaspoon (about 5 grams) for a week, then increase gradually to 10 grams, which is enough for its effect on the gut.
Drink enough water with it.
Try it for 4 weeks, then judge its effect on you.
Safety
Generally safe in food amounts.
In the first week: Bloating, gas, nausea or soft stools in many people, usually easing within days. In the sickle cell trial, about a third of patients had mild symptoms that went away within a week.
Medicines: It reduces the absorption of some, and a Sudanese study found it reduces the absorption of the antibiotic amoxicillin. Take it 2 hours apart from any medicine.
Kidney patients: Only with the kidney doctor's approval, especially those whose fluid intake is restricted or who are on dialysis.
Pregnancy, breastfeeding and children: Food amounts only; therapeutic amounts have not been studied in them.
Allergy to it is rare, mostly asthma in people who breathe in its dust at work.
Buying and quality
Good hashab: Hard round lumps, from yellowish white to light amber, odourless, with a mild taste.
Soaked in cold water, it slowly dissolves into a clear, sticky liquid with no residue.
Beware of very dark lumps or lumps mixed with sand and bark, and powder of unknown origin that may be mixed with starch or sugar.

p:gut:0:0.x: The topic «Maryam» visitors search for most. Here is the difference between IBS and other conditions, what actually helps according to the evidence, foods on our table that trigger bloating and their alternatives, herbs and their limits, and when to see a doctor.

p:gut:1:0.t: Colon and bloating — See a doctor before trying any remedy if
p:gut:1:0.x:
Blood in the stool or black stool, or anaemia on a blood test.
Unexplained weight loss.
Symptoms starting for the first time after age 40, or a lasting change in bowel habit.
Diarrhoea that wakes you from sleep, or fever with abdominal pain.
A family history of colon cancer, inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease.
Women over 50: persistent, almost daily bloating or feeling full quickly, which needs an ovarian check.
Severe persistent pain, repeated vomiting, or a swollen belly with no passing of wind or stool: go to the emergency department now.

p:gut:2:0.t: Colon and bloating — What do people call «the colon»?
p:gut:2:0.x:
Irritable bowel
Abdominal pain or cramps that recur and are linked to bowel movements, with constipation, diarrhoea or both, and bloating. The bowel looks normal on tests but is sensitive and its movement is disturbed. It is chronic, calms and flares, does not turn into cancer and does not damage the bowel.
Ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease
True inflammation of the bowel: diarrhoea with blood or mucus, weight loss, sometimes fever, and it can wake you at night. It needs a gastroenterologist and regular treatment; changing your diet is not enough.
Coeliac disease (wheat allergy)
An immune disease triggered by the protein in wheat and barley (gluten). Its symptoms resemble IBS: bloating, diarrhoea, tiredness and anaemia. It is detected by a blood test, so do not stop eating bread before the test, as that spoils the result.
Lactose intolerance
Many adults do not digest milk sugar well, so milk causes gas and diarrhoea. Yoghurt, laban and aged cheese are usually easier, and lactose-free dairy is available.
Chronic constipation
Fewer than three bowel movements a week, or hard stool passed with straining. It gets worse with too little water and movement and with putting off going to the toilet.
Colon cancer
In the UAE it is diagnosed about 15 years earlier than in the West: the median age at diagnosis is 55, compared with 70 in America. So the Abu Dhabi Department of Health recommends starting screening at 40, even without symptoms. Ask your doctor about a stool test or colonoscopy.

p:gut:3:0.t: Colon and bloating — What actually helps
p:gut:3:0.x:
Relatively strong Soluble fibre: psyllium (isabgol) and oats. Start with a small amount and increase gradually with plenty of water. Coarse bran, on the other hand, can make bloating worse.
Moderate Peppermint oil in enteric-coated capsules: eases pain and bloating in the short term. Not suitable if you have heartburn, reflux or a hiatus hernia.
Moderate A temporary low-FODMAP diet under the guidance of a dietitian; details further down the page.
Moderate Gut-directed psychological therapy: cognitive behavioural therapy or gut-directed hypnotherapy. Not because the pain is imaginary, but because the brain and gut are connected.
Moderate Movement: a daily walk improves bowel movements and eases bloating.
Moderate Regular meals: meals at set times without rushing, without skipping meals or leaving long gaps between them.
Moderate Water: 8 cups a day at least, more in the Gulf heat, and no more than 3 cups of tea and coffee.
Limited Probiotics: results are mixed. If you try them, continue for at least 4 weeks, then assess, and stop if they do not help.
Limited Flaxseed: up to 1 tablespoon a day, ground, may help constipation and bloating.

p:gut:4:0.t: Colon and bloating — By your type of IBS
p:gut:4:0.x:
If constipation dominates
Water, psyllium or flaxseed introduced gradually, two kiwis a day, and walking. Do not put off going to the toilet, and rest your feet on a small stool when sitting.
If diarrhoea dominates
Cut down on coffee, fatty and spicy food and sugar-free sweeteners, try psyllium, drink enough water, and use oral rehydration solution with severe diarrhoea. Diarrhoea that wakes you at night or contains blood needs a doctor.
If bloating dominates
Eat slowly and chew well, cut down on fizzy drinks and chewing gum, walk a little after eating, and do not lie down straight after a meal.

p:gut:5:0.t: Colon and bloating — Foods on our table that may trigger bloating
p:gut:5:0.x:
Not every patient reacts to all of them. Try and observe, and avoid only what triggers you.
Food	Why	Alternative or solution
Onion and garlic	Among the commonest triggers of gas in people with IBS.	Try the green part of spring onions, and oil in which garlic was fried and then removed.
Chickpeas, lentils and fava beans	They contain sugars that ferment in the gut.	Small portions; well-rinsed canned ones are easier, and long soaking helps.
Wheat bread and pastries	Triggers bloating in some people.	Rice, potatoes and oats; long-fermented sourdough bread is easier for some.
Milk	Lactose (milk sugar).	Yoghurt and laban, or lactose-free milk.
Dates and honey	In large amounts they can trigger bloating in some people.	Do not ban them: one or two dates at a sitting and a teaspoon of honey, and watch how you feel.
Apples, pears, mango and watermelon	They contain sugars that cause gas in sensitive people.	Bananas, oranges, grapes, strawberries and kiwi are easier; no more than 3 portions of fruit a day.
Chewing gum and sweets labelled «sugar-free»	They contain sweeteners such as sorbitol that cause diarrhoea and gas.	Read the ingredients and avoid them.
Fizzy drinks and energy drinks	Gas and caffeine.	Water and mint infusion.
Coffee and strong tea	Caffeine stimulates the bowel and worsens diarrhoea in some people.	3 cups a day at most.
Large, fatty meals	They slow digestion and increase cramping.	Smaller meals. In Ramadan: break the fast with dates and water, then pray, then eat the meal.

p:gut:6:0.x:

p:gut:7:0.t: Colon and bloating — The low-FODMAP diet in brief
p:gut:7:0.x:
«FODMAP» is a name for short sugars that ferment in the gut and cause gas and pain in people with IBS. They are found in onion, garlic, wheat, legumes, milk and some fruits. The diet has three stages:
Reduce them all for two to six weeks.
Bring them back one at a time to find out what harms you.
A long-term diet that avoids only what triggers you.
Do not stay on the first stage for long: it makes the diet poorer and reduces beneficial gut bacteria. It is best done with a dietitian.

p:gut:8:0.t: Colon and bloating — The gut and stress
p:gut:8:0.x:
The gut has a network of nerves connected to the brain, which is why IBS flares with stress, poor sleep, exams and travel. Enough sleep, walking, slow breathing and psychological therapy with a specialist for those with long-standing symptoms all help.
In the hadith: «Talbina soothes the heart of the sick and takes away some of the grief» (narrated by al-Bukhari). Talbina is made from barley, so anyone whose bloating is triggered by barley should have less of it.

p:gut:9:0.x: For two weeks, write down what you ate, when you slept, when you were stressed and when the symptoms came. You will usually find two or three triggers of your own, instead of avoiding half your food. Take the diary with you to the doctor.

p:gut:10:0.x:
«IBS turns into cancer»
It does not, and it does not shorten life. But new symptoms after 40 deserve testing.
«All bloating is the colon»
It may be lactose intolerance, coeliac disease, constipation or another illness.
«Colon cleansing removes toxins»
There is no evidence for it. Coffee or herbal enemas can cause dehydration, salt imbalance and bowel perforation.
«Give up bread and milk completely»
Avoid only what is proven to trigger you, and test for coeliac disease before giving up bread.
«A food sensitivity test reveals what harms you»
The widely sold antibody (IgG) tests are not reliable for this and make you avoid foods for no reason.
«The guaranteed colon blend»
Some unknown blends contain strong laxatives or hidden drugs. Beware of anyone who promises a complete cure.

This page is for education and does not replace a doctor. IBS is diagnosed by a doctor after ruling out other conditions, and the doctor prescribes the right treatment for your case.

p:dent:0:0.x: Our heritage has long cared for the mouth, from the miswak to clove and myrrh. Here is what holds up and what harms, the causes of the most common mouth problems, the daily care that really protects the teeth, and when to see a doctor.

p:dent:1:0.t: Mouth and teeth — See a dentist without delay if
p:dent:1:0.x:
Swelling of the face, jaw or under the eye, or fever with toothache: it may be an abscess that needs a dentist the same day.
Swelling spreading to the neck, or difficulty swallowing, breathing or opening the mouth: go to the emergency department immediately.
A permanent tooth knocked out by a blow: hold it by the crown, not the root, rinse it with water without scrubbing, put it back in place or keep it in milk, and see a dentist within an hour.
Bleeding that does not stop after a tooth extraction despite pressing on clean gauze for half an hour.
An ulcer or a white or red patch in the mouth that does not heal within two weeks, especially in people who smoke or use medwakh or chewing tobacco.
Bleeding gums with bruises on the body or severe tiredness: a blood test is needed.

p:dent:2:0.t: Mouth and teeth — Common mouth problems
p:dent:2:0.x:
Toothache
It is usually caused by decay that has reached the nerve, an abscess, or a cracked tooth. Clove eases it for a few hours only; the treatment is a filling or root canal treatment at the dentist. Pain that settles by itself may mean the nerve has died, not that it has healed.
Bleeding and inflamed gums
The main cause is the layer of bacteria (plaque) at the gum line. The treatment is better cleaning with the brush and floss, not stopping cleaning for fear of the blood. If it lasts two weeks, the tartar needs cleaning at the dentist. Diabetes increases gum inflammation, and gum inflammation makes blood sugar harder to control.
Bad breath
Most of it comes from the mouth itself: debris on the tongue, decay and gum inflammation. Clean your tongue and drink water. It gets worse with dryness and fasting, and the hadith says: «The smell of the fasting person's mouth is better with Allah than the scent of musk» (Bukhari and Muslim). Breath that stays bad despite cleaning needs a dentist.
Mouth ulcers (white sores)
Small painful sores that heal by themselves within one to two weeks. They are triggered by stress, biting the cheek, sour and spicy food, and lack of iron or vitamin B12. Honey and rinsing with salt water soothe them; frequent recurring ones need a blood test.
Dry mouth
From not drinking enough water, mouth breathing, diabetes, and many medicines including those for blood pressure, allergy and depression. It increases decay and bad breath. Sip water often, and tell your doctor if it started with a new medicine.
Sensitive teeth
A short pain with cold or sweet things. It comes from worn enamel or receding gums, and is made worse by hard scrubbing, citrus and fizzy drinks. A soft brush and a toothpaste for sensitive teeth help; persistent sensitivity needs a check-up.

p:dent:3:0.t: Mouth and teeth — Daily care that really works
p:dent:3:0.x:
Relatively strong Brush twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste, for two minutes, most importantly before bed. Spit out the toothpaste and do not rinse much with water, so the fluoride stays on the teeth.
Relatively strong Cut down how often you have sugar, not just how much. Sweets, juice and sweetened tea between meals do more harm than having them with a meal.
Relatively strong Quitting smoking, medwakh, shisha and chewing tobacco: among the biggest causes of gum disease, tooth loss and mouth cancer.
Moderate The miswak: A 2022 scientific review found it reduces plaque and gum inflammation about as well as a toothbrush, and better when used together with the brush. Still brush with fluoride at least once a day, because fluoride protects against decay.
Moderate Floss or an interdental brush once a day, because the toothbrush does not reach between the teeth.
Moderate Cleaning the tongue with the brush or a scraper reduces bad breath.
Moderate Visiting the dentist every 6 to 12 months for a check-up and tartar cleaning, even without pain.
Limited Herbal mouth rinses such as sage and green tea: they may help the gums, but they are an addition, not a substitute for the toothbrush.

p:dent:4:0.t: Mouth and teeth — Herbs and the mouth
p:dent:4:0.x:
All

p:dent:6:0.t: Mouth and teeth — Children's teeth and teething
p:dent:6:0.x:
From the first tooth
Clean them with a small brush and a smear of fluoride toothpaste the size of a grain of rice, and from 3 years the size of a pea. Brush your child's teeth yourself until they can do it well, around 7 years.
The bottle at bedtime
Do not let a child fall asleep with a bottle of milk or juice in the mouth; this is one of the biggest causes of decay in baby teeth. Water alone does no harm.
Teething
A firm rubber teether, chilled but not frozen, and massaging the gums with a clean finger. No amber necklaces, as choking and deaths have been recorded with them, no numbing gel for babies, no honey under one year, and no clove oil.
Is the fever from teething?
Teething may raise the temperature slightly, but a high fever or severe diarrhoea is usually not from it, so see the doctor.

p:dent:7:0.x:
«An aspirin tablet on the aching tooth»
Aspirin does not relieve pain from the outside; it burns the gum and leaves a painful white sore.
«Garlic on the tooth»
It burns the gum and cheek and causes sores, and it does not treat decay.
«Lemon, baking soda or charcoal for whitening»
Acid dissolves the enamel and coarse powder scratches it, so the teeth turn more yellow and become sensitive. A slight yellow tint is normal, and safe whitening is done at the dentist.
«Oil pulling treats decay and removes toxins»
The evidence is weak; it does not replace the toothbrush and does not remove toxins from the body. Do not swallow the oil afterwards.
«Bleeding gums mean I should stop brushing»
The opposite: bleeding is a sign of inflammation from bacteria, and gentle regular cleaning stops it within days.
«Baby teeth do not matter because they will fall out»
Decay in them hurts the child, may harm the permanent teeth underneath, and affects eating and speech.
«Opening or cauterising an abscess at home»
It may spread the infection to the face and the blood. An abscess needs a dentist.
«Medwakh is milder than cigarettes»
It is concentrated tobacco, and all forms of tobacco raise the risk of gum disease and mouth cancer.

European Medicines Agency: sage leaf
This page is for education and does not replace the dentist. Herbs may ease pain or inflammation for a while, but decay, abscesses and tartar can only be treated by the dentist.

p:ker:0:0.x: The state of Kerala in southern India is one of the world's best-known centres of traditional Indian medicine, «Ayurveda», and many of its practitioners in the UAE come from there. Here is some of its history, what helps and what harms among its well-known treatments, and recipes from it that suit our homes.

p:ker:1:0.t: Kerala medicine (Ayurveda) — Before any Ayurvedic treatment
p:ker:1:0.x:
Snakebite: go to hospital immediately for antivenom. Do not waste time with a traditional healer, and do not cut, suck or tightly tie the bite.
Do not stop medicines for diabetes, blood pressure, the heart or epilepsy for an Ayurvedic treatment.
Pregnant and breastfeeding women and children: no Ayurvedic preparations without the doctor's approval.
Metallic «bhasma» preparations: do not take them, as heavy metals are added to them on purpose.
Treatment by vomiting, purging or enemas («panchakarma») is dangerous for older people and heart and kidney patients, and must only be done under medical supervision.

p:ker:2:0.t: Kerala medicine (Ayurveda) — From the history of Kerala medicine
p:ker:2:0.x:
The book «Ashtanga Hridayam»
One of the best-known classical texts of Indian medicine, by Vagbhata
The book Kerala's physicians relied on; they used to learn its 7,120 verses by heart.
The eight physicians, the «Ashtavaidyas»
Hereditary families of Kerala
Eight Namboothiri Brahmin families who mastered the eight branches of medicine; four of them still practise. They wrote books in Malayalam such as «Sahasrayogam» and «Chikitsamanjari».
«Hortus Malabaricus» (The Garden of Malabar)
1678–1703
An encyclopedia of plants in 12 volumes, with about 742 Kerala plants and 794 engravings. It was compiled by the Dutch governor Van Rheede, and the folk healer Itty Achudan dictated its knowledge in Malayalam. It also records the plant names in Arabic.
Arya Vaidya Sala in Kottakkal
1902
Founded by the physician P. S. Varier, it turned household remedies into medicines made in factories, and Kerala became a world centre of Ayurveda.
Kerala and the Arabs
Centuries of trade
From Kerala's Malabar coast, black pepper, cardamom, ginger and turmeric reached our kitchens with Arab traders. That is why Kerala's herbs are close to the herbs of our own homes.

p:ker:6:0.x:

p:afr:0:0.x: Africa is a vast continent with thousands of medicinal plants, and much of what is in our homes came from it: frankincense, myrrh, gum arabic, hibiscus and coffee. Here is a look at traditional medicine there today, and what helps and what harms among its best-known remedies.

p:afr:1:0.t: Traditional African medicine — Before any traditional treatment
p:afr:1:0.x:
Fever after travelling to Africa, even weeks later: see a doctor immediately and tell them about your trip, as it may be malaria. Do not rely on herbs, and before travelling ask the doctor about prevention.
Snakebite: go to hospital immediately for antivenom, not to a traditional healer.
Do not abandon treatment for HIV, tuberculosis, diabetes or blood pressure for a herbal blend.
Do not use unknown roots or powders as enemas, and do not give them to children.
Pregnant and breastfeeding women and children: no blends without the doctor's approval.

p:afr:2:0.t: Traditional African medicine — Traditional medicine in Africa
p:afr:2:0.x:
Traditional medicine in Africa today
World Health Organization
About 80% of Africa's population relies on traditional medicine for basic health needs. Today more than 40 African countries have a national policy regulating it, up from only 8 in 2000.
African Traditional Medicine Day
31 August, since 2003
An annual day marked by African countries with the World Health Organization, calling for the study of African herbs and the regulation of traditional healers.
Africa and the Arabs
Centuries of trade
Frankincense and myrrh came from the Horn of Africa, and gum arabic, hibiscus and baobab from Sudan. Coffee travelled from Abyssinia to Yemen and then to the world.
From South Africa to European pharmacies
Umckaloabo
The root of the African geranium became one of the best-known herbal cough medicines in Germany: an example of a traditional herb that entered research, though its evidence is still weak.
Sweet wormwood and malaria
The difference between a plant and a medicine
Artemisinin, the basis of modern malaria medicines, was extracted from this plant. But drinking the plant itself does not cure, because a medicine is a precise, pure dose and the plant is not.

p:afr:3:0.t: Traditional African medicine — Well-known African remedies: what helps and what harms

p:skin:0:0.x: Tradition holds many skin remedies; some help, and some leave lifelong scars. Here is some of their history, which folk practices help or harm, common skin conditions in the Gulf heat, and signs that need a doctor.

p:skin:1:0.t: Skin in Tradition — See a doctor or go to emergency immediately if
p:skin:1:0.x:
A rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass, especially with fever: go to emergency immediately, and do not wait for a rash if the person is very ill. On dark skin, check the palms and soles.
A burn larger than the person's hand, or with blisters on the face, hands or genitals, or a deep or electrical burn.
Eczema that weeps, has pus or crusts, becomes hot and painful, spreads fast, or comes with fever.
A new mole, or one changing in shape, colour or size: see a dermatologist without delay.

p:skin:2:0.t: Skin in Tradition — From the history of skin diseases
p:skin:2:0.x:
Ancient Egypt: the Ebers Papyrus
around 1550 BCE
Among its roughly 700 recipes are remedies for skin diseases, using honey and many plants, mixed with incantations.
Abu Bakr al-Razi: «Smallpox and Measles»
9th–10th century CE
He described both diseases from the signs he saw in his patients and told them apart; both are fevers that bring a rash on the skin. The book was translated into Latin and shaped the treatment of smallpox in Europe until the seventeenth century. It also gave recipes to remove smallpox marks, which historians believe did not work, given how many people kept the scars on their faces.
The end of smallpox
In 1980
The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated after vaccination campaigns, the first disease ever wiped out among humans. What centuries of recipes could not do, vaccination did.

p:skin:3:0.t: Skin in Tradition — Folk habits: what is right and what harms
p:skin:3:0.x:
All
Sound
With care
Harmful
Habit	In heritage	Today
Cooling a burn under running water
Sound	The first thing to do for a burn.	Running water for at least 20 minutes, then cover with cling film. Do not pop blisters.
Emollients instead of soap for eczema
Sound	Rubbing dry skin with oils is an old practice.	Emollients at least twice a day, and used to wash instead of soap. They make clothing catch fire more easily, so keep away from flames.
Shade and loose clothing
Sound	Turbans and covering clothes in the heat.	They protect against heat rash, sunburn and melasma: loose cotton clothes, a wide-brimmed hat, and staying somewhere cool.
Honey on minor burns
With care	Honey is one of the oldest things put on wounds.	Cochrane review (2008): it may speed healing of mild to moderate superficial burns, but all its trials came from one centre. Apply after cooling; a large burn needs a doctor.
Aloe vera gel on burns
With care	Common in folk medicine.	Review (2007) of four trials: it may speed healing of first- and second-degree burns, but the evidence is not conclusive.
Fig sap on warts and eczema
With care	One of the best-known folk skin remedies.	It contains substances (furocoumarins) that cause burns and blisters if the skin is exposed to sun. Apply with a glove to a small spot, keep the area out of the sun, and never use on children.
Massaging newborns with olive oil
With care	A widespread habit to soften a baby's skin.	A trial (2015) of 115 babies: olive and sunflower oil delayed the maturing of the skin barrier, and the researchers advised against using them on healthy baby skin.
Ice, butter or toothpaste on a burn
Harmful	«To cool the burn».	Never put ice, cream or oil on a burn. Running water is the first treatment.
Toothpaste on pimples
Harmful	«Dries the pimple».	Dermatologists advise against it: it irritates the skin and can cause a chemical burn.
Squeezing pimples and blackheads
Harmful	«Cleans the face».	It worsens acne and leaves scars.
Lemon on the skin, then sun
Harmful	To lighten skin and freckles.	It causes a blistering rash and dark patches that last weeks or months. Wash your hands after squeezing lemons before going into the sun.
Fig leaves or their decoction for tanning
Harmful	For a quick tan.	Severe burns have been recorded after fig-leaf decoctions and tanning lotions made from them.
Black henna
Harmful	A quick, long-lasting black design.	It contains a chemical dye (PPD) that causes blisters, allergy and scars; a case in Kuwait had blisters in the exact shape of the design. Natural henna is reddish-brown.
Unknown lightening creams

p:skin:3:1.t: Skin in Tradition — Folk habits: what is right and what harms
p:skin:3:1.x:
Harmful	«Instant whitening».	Some contain mercury, which harms the kidneys and causes rash, patches and scars. Steroid creams used without a doctor cause acne, thin skin and stretch marks; in a study in Iraq, 65.7% of patients used them for lightening.
Kerosene or petrol for lice
Harmful	An old home remedy.	It causes burns and eye injuries, and can catch fire. A fine-tooth comb first, and a pharmacist can advise on treatment.

p:skin:4:0.t: Skin in Tradition — Common skin conditions here
p:skin:4:0.x:
Eczema
Dryness, itching and inflammation that come and go. Basic care: emollients at least twice a day and instead of soap, and avoiding triggers. Do not change diet except under a doctor's supervision.
Acne
Caused by hormones and genes, not poor hygiene, and there is no evidence that food causes it. Wash the face no more than twice a day with a gentle cleanser and lukewarm water, and do not squeeze spots. See a doctor if nodules or cysts appear, to avoid scarring. Treatment can take up to three months.
Athlete's foot
Common in heat and humidity. Prevention: dry feet well, including between the toes, do not share towels or shoes, and wear flip-flops in public showers. A pharmacist can advise on treatment, which continues two weeks after the rash clears.
Heat rash
Small itchy spots in heat and humidity. Eased by cooling down, loose cotton clothes, drinking fluids, a cold compress for up to 20 minutes, patting rather than scratching, and avoiding perfumed products. See a doctor if it does not improve within a few days.
Melasma
Brown patches on the face, harmless, not contagious and never turning into cancer. Triggered by sun, pregnancy and the contraceptive pill. The key treatment is sun protection: a wide hat and high-protection sunscreen. Nothing cures it for good and it may return, so beware of creams promising quick whitening.
Vitiligo
White patches, not contagious, caused by the body's immune system attacking the skin's pigment cells. The patches burn easily in the sun, so protect them with high-protection sunscreen (50) and clothing. A dermatologist has treatments for it.
Psoriasis
A chronic, non-contagious disease. Triggered by stress, smoking, obesity, some medicines, infections and skin injury. Regular emollients ease the scales, and moderate sun may help without excess. Anyone with joint pain or swelling should tell a doctor soon.
Moles and skin cancer
Watch for a mole that is asymmetrical, has an irregular border, mixed colours, a diameter over 6 mm, or changes over time. Any one of these needs a dermatologist right away.
Chronic skin conditions such as eczema, psoriasis and vitiligo are controlled over time and do not vanish with one mixture. Beware of anyone promising a full cure; a dermatologist is the reference.

Wild trees and herbs of our environment: where they grow, what our people used them for, and what UAE health authorities say about their safety.
Mind the names: «Harmal» in the Gulf is a different plant from the harmal of the Levant and North Africa, and «jaadah» in the UAE is a different species from that of the Levant. One name can mean two plants, so don't rely on the name alone.
All
Known use
Safety unknown
Poisonous or dangerous
Ghaf
Prosopis cineraria · Desert
Safety unknown
The national tree of the UAE since 2008. It withstands drought, can live about 120 years, and is threatened by urban growth and overgrazing.
Safety: Its folk medicinal uses have not been tested in people. It is one of the most important trees in our environment, so don't cut it or break its branches.
Ghaf Photos ↗ Source: The tree's page at the Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi
Sidr (Christ's thorn jujube) (Nabq)
Ziziphus spina-christi · Mountains and wadis
Known use
A thorny tree with oval leaves and round orange or yellow fruit. Used traditionally for cough and fever, and for washing hair and caring for the skin.
Safety: The dried fruit is likely safe up to 30 grams a day. Not to be drunk during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
Sidr Photos ↗ Source: Public information leaflet on the plant from the Abu Dhabi Department of Health
Samr (umbrella thorn)
Vachellia tortilis · Plains, mountains and wadis
A thorny, umbrella-shaped tree 4–6 metres tall, with coiled pods.
Photos ↗ Source: guide to the wild plants of the UAE
Shua (wild moringa) (Ban, Yasar)
Moringa peregrina · Mountains and wadis, especially in Ru'us al-Jibal
Safety unknown
Its seeds and oil are used traditionally for headache, fever, abdominal pain, constipation, burns and back pain, with no good scientific evidence for these uses.
Safety: The root and bark are unsafe because they contain toxic substances. The leaves, fruit and seeds eaten as food are likely safe.
Moringa Photos ↗ Source: Public information leaflet on the plant from the Abu Dhabi Department of Health
Arak (toothbrush tree) (Miswak)
Salvadora persica · Rare in the wild, but widely planted on farms and along roads as a windbreak
Known use
Its twigs have been used as miswak to clean teeth since ancient times, and it was used traditionally for toothache, gum and joint pain, and constipation.
Safety: Brushing with it is safe. Do not eat or drink it during pregnancy or breastfeeding, as little is known about its safety.
Miswak Photos ↗ Source: Public information leaflet on the plant from the Abu Dhabi Department of Health
Qurm (grey mangrove) (Shura, mangrove)

p:uae:0:1.x:
Avicennia marina · Shores and creeks, including Khor Kalba
Safety unknown
A tree growing in coastal mud, with roots that stick up above the mud to breathe. Its leaves feed camels, its bees make good honey, and its bark and leaves were used in folk medicine.
Safety: Little research has been done, and there are no data on its safety in people.
Photos ↗ Source: The plant's page in the Encyclopedia of Medicinal Plants of the UAE, from the Abu Dhabi Department of Health
Markh (broom bush) (Fire tree)
Leptadenia pyrotechnica · Sands and low dunes in eastern Abu Dhabi and the northern emirates
Safety unknown
Burned as incense for rheumatism, joint pain, sciatica and back pain, and its stem was used for kidney stones. Its dried seed hairs were used to light fires.
Safety: There is no safety guidance for people, and studies are only in animals.

Gulf harmal (Adfir)
Rhazya stricta
Poisonous or dangerous
Its decoction is drunk traditionally for headache, stomach, rheumatism, skin and worms. It is different from the «harmal» of the Levant and North Africa (Peganum harmala), and both are poisonous.
Safety: Rich in alkaloids; drinking it is likely unsafe, and it must be avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
Photos ↗ Source: Public information leaflet on the plant from the Abu Dhabi Department of Health
Ja'dah (felty germander)
Teucrium stocksianum · Rocky areas
Poisonous or dangerous
Drunk traditionally for stomach and bowel pain, colds, fever, kidney problems and to lower blood sugar.

Ushar (Sodom's apple)
Calotropis procera · Plains and desert
Poisonous or dangerous
A shrub with leaves covered in white fuzz and a sticky white sap.
Safety: Poisonous.

Poisonous or dangerous

An ornamental with sticky white sap, long fruit and seeds with feathery hairs.

Safety: All parts are poisonous, especially the leaves, and it affects the heartbeat.

Period pain
One of the most common things women treat with herbs. The strongest evidence is for ginger, heat and exercise; small trials suggest cinnamon and fennel help too.
Herbs and supplements
Ginger

What helps
Start ginger on the first day, or a day before your period, as it works better than waiting for the pain to get bad.
Put a warm compress or hot-water bottle on your lower belly for 20 minutes.
Regular walking and light exercise throughout the month reduce pain.
Avoid
Don't take large amounts of Chinese (cassia) cinnamon daily for long periods.
Don't put up with pain that stops you studying or working every month as if it were normal.
See a doctor if:
The pain is severe and does not ease, or gets worse year after year.
Pain that started after age 25 when it wasn't there before, or pain during sex.
Bleeding between periods, fever or unusual discharge.
Premenstrual syndrome (PMS)
Mood swings, bloating and breast tenderness in the days before a period. The best-studied herb is chasteberry (vitex), followed by saffron in small trials.
Herbs and supplements
Chasteberry
Saffron
Chamomile
Evening primrose oil
Blends in this guide
Recipe: Chamomile and mint for period bloating
What helps
Track your symptoms for two months to see the pattern; it helps your doctor too.
Cut down on salt, caffeine and sugar in the week before your period.
Calcium from food (milk, yoghurt, sesame) and exercise both have good evidence.
Regular sleep eases mood swings.
Avoid
Don't combine chasteberry with the contraceptive pill, fertility treatment or antipsychotics without a doctor.

p:women:0:1.x:
Evening primrose oil hasn't been shown to help this condition, so don't spend much on it.
See a doctor if:
Deep sadness or thoughts of self-harm before your period; this may be a treatable mood disorder.
Symptoms damage your relationships or work every month.
Irregular periods and PCOS
Polycystic ovary syndrome is very common in the Gulf. The main treatment is losing a little weight (5–10% is often enough) and staying active; herbs only help alongside. Small studies suggest spearmint tea reduces unwanted hair and cinnamon may make cycles more regular.
Herbs and supplements
Mint
Cinnamon
Chasteberry
Flaxseed
Blends in this guide
Recipe: Spearmint tea for PCOS
Recipe: Cinnamon tea for periods
What helps
Cut down on sugar and white bread, and eat more vegetables, pulses and protein.
Walk for 30 minutes on most days of the week.
Have your HbA1c, thyroid and hormones checked by your doctor.
Avoid
Don't rely on “hormone balancing” blends of unknown content.
Don't use herbs instead of treatment if you're trying to conceive; see your doctor.
See a doctor if:
No period for more than 3 months without pregnancy.
Excess facial and body hair, severe acne, or hair thinning on the scalp.
Difficulty conceiving after a year of trying (or 6 months after age 35).
Heavy periods and anaemia
Heavy periods are the most common cause of iron deficiency in women. Dates, date syrup and spinach help, but they can't make up for a large iron deficit.
Herbs and supplements
Dates and fresh dates
Iron
Vitamin C
Moringa
Nettle
What helps
Eat iron sources with something rich in vitamin C (lemon, orange, peppers) to boost absorption.
Drink tea and coffee an hour away from meals.
Check your haemoglobin and iron stores (ferritin) once a year.
Avoid
Don't take iron tablets for long periods without testing.
Don't take herbs “to stop bleeding” instead of getting a diagnosis.
See a doctor if:
Changing your pad every hour or less for several hours, or clots bigger than a coin.
Periods longer than 7 days, or dizziness, palpitations and severe tiredness.
Any bleeding after your periods have stopped for good (menopause).
Urinary tract infections
Recurrent burning when passing urine is common in women. Cranberry may reduce repeat infections for some, but it doesn't treat an active infection; that needs antibiotics.

Cranberry
Corn silk
Parsley
Blends in this guide

What helps
Drink plenty of water and don't hold in urine.
Pass urine after sex, and wipe from front to back.
Cranberry juice or capsules for prevention if infections keep coming back.
Avoid

p:women:0:2.x:
Don't rely on diuretic herbs alone if there is burning and fever.
Don't take large amounts of cranberry with warfarin.
See a doctor if:
Fever, shivering, or pain in the side or back (possible kidney infection).
Blood in the urine.
Any urinary symptoms during pregnancy: see your doctor the same day.
Intimate hygiene and discharge
The vagina cleans itself, and most folk remedies here do more harm than good. Itching and smelly discharge need a diagnosis, because thrush is treated differently from bacterial infection.
What helps
Wash the outer area with water or a gentle unscented wash.
Wear cotton underwear and avoid staying in wet clothes.
Yoghurt in your diet is part of healthy eating, but the evidence for prevention is limited.
Avoid
Don't douche; it upsets the natural balance and increases infections.
Don't sit over herbal steam (vaginal steaming); it has caused burns and has no proven benefit.
Don't put garlic, essential oils, vinegar or herbs inside the vagina.
Don't use perfumes or scented sprays on the intimate area.
See a doctor if:
Discharge of unusual colour or smell, or itching that doesn't clear within days.
Pelvic pain or fever.
Any symptoms during pregnancy.
Pregnancy: what helps and what to avoid
The time to be most careful with herbs. Ginger for pregnancy sickness is well studied, and folic acid is essential before and in early pregnancy. Many common herbs can cause contractions or harm the baby in medicinal amounts.

Ginger
Folic acid
Dates and fresh dates
Iron
Blends in this guide

What helps
Folic acid 400 micrograms a day from before pregnancy until the end of the third month, or as your doctor advises.
For nausea: small frequent meals, and ginger in moderate amounts (up to about 1 gram a day).
Herbs used as spices in food are generally safe; be careful with medicinal doses and capsules.
Ask your doctor or pharmacist before any herb or supplement.
Avoid
Avoid completely: pennyroyal, harmal (Syrian rue), wormwood and mugwort, senna, and myrrh in large amounts.

First steps until you reach medical help. In any serious situation, call your country's ambulance first. Every home is advised to take a first-aid and CPR course.
Snakebite
Scorpion sting
Dog, cat or any animal bite
Severe bleeding and deep wounds
Minor wounds and scratches
Boils and abscesses

Burns
