 Emergency now ·  Doctor the same day ·  Usually treated at home
Snakebite
Emergency now
Do
Call an ambulance immediately or go to the nearest hospital; the treatment is antivenom.
Move away from the snake, and do not try to catch or kill it. Photograph it from a distance if you can do so safely.
Keep the person as calm and still as possible, as movement spreads the venom.
Immobilise the bitten limb with a splint or sling, roughly at heart level.
Remove rings, watches and tight clothing before swelling starts.
Note the time of the bite.
Don't
Do not cut the bite or suck out the venom.
Do not tie the limb with a rope or tourniquet.
Do not apply ice, burn the area or use electric shocks.
Do not apply herbs, garlic, harmal or kerosene.
Do not give stimulants or alcohol, and do not wait for symptoms to appear.
Go to the emergency department if:
Treat every snakebite as an emergency until proven otherwise.
Scorpion sting
Doctor the same day
Do
Wash the sting with soap and water.
Apply a cold compress (ice wrapped in cloth) for 10 minutes, then remove it, and repeat.
Keep the stung limb still at heart level.
Go to hospital — children, older people and heart patients always and immediately, as they are most at risk of complications.
Don't
Do not cut or suck the sting.
Do not tie the limb.
Do not burn the area or apply herbs, garlic or kerosene.
Do not kill the scorpion with your hand; photograph it if possible.
Go to the emergency department if:
Heavy sweating, drooling or vomiting.
Muscle twitching or abnormal eye movements.
Difficulty breathing or swallowing.
Severe agitation or constant crying in a child.
Dog, cat or any animal bite
Doctor the same day
Do
Wash the wound at once under running water with soap for a full 15 minutes; this is one of the most important protections against rabies.
Apply an antiseptic such as iodine or alcohol after washing.
Cover the wound with a clean dressing.
Go to hospital the same day; you may need urgent preventive treatment against rabies and tetanus.
Remember details of the animal: is it a pet and vaccinated? Where is it now?
Don't

p:aid:0:1.x:
Do not stitch or close the wound at home.
Do not apply coffee, soil, pepper or herbs.
Do not ignore a cat bite; it gets infected more often than a dog bite.
Do not wait for symptoms: rabies is fatal once symptoms appear, and hospital treatment straight after the bite prevents it.
Go to the emergency department if:
A deep bite, a bite on the face or hands, or bleeding that will not stop.
A bite from a wild or stray animal or a bat.
Spreading redness, pus or fever in the following days.
Severe bleeding and deep wounds
Emergency now
Do
Call an ambulance.
Press hard and directly on the wound with a clean cloth for at least 10 minutes without lifting it to look.
If the cloth soaks through, put another on top and do not remove the first.
Raise the injured limb above heart level if possible.
Keep the person lying down and warm.
Don't
Do not remove an object stuck in the wound; secure it and press around it.
Do not apply coffee, ash or toothpaste to stop bleeding.
Do not use a tourniquet except for life-threatening bleeding in an arm or leg, and only by a trained person.
Go to the emergency department if:
Blood gushing strongly or pulsing.
Bleeding that does not stop after 10 minutes of pressure.
A deep wound with gaping edges, on the face, or contaminated with soil or rust.
Minor wounds and scratches
Usually treated at home
Do
Wash your hands first.
Rinse the wound under clean running water for 5 minutes, and clean around it with soap.
Press with a clean cloth if it is bleeding until it stops.
Cover with a clean dressing, and change it daily or when wet.
Sterile medical honey helps scratches heal (see the recipe).
Don't
Do not put coffee, turmeric, toothpaste or soil on an open wound.
Do not put cotton wool directly on the wound, as its fibres stick to it.
Do not use kitchen honey on open wounds.
Go to the emergency department if:
Signs of infection: spreading redness, red streaks, pus or fever.
A dirty wound and no tetanus vaccine for more than 5 years.
A wound that has not healed after two weeks, especially in people with diabetes.
Recipe: Medical honey for superficial wounds
Boils and abscesses
Usually treated at home
Do
Apply a warm compress for 10–15 minutes, 3–4 times a day; it helps the boil come to a head and drain on its own.
Keep the area clean and cover it with a clean dressing once it drains.
Wash your hands well after touching it.
Use your own towel and wash it in hot water.
Don't
Do not squeeze the boil or prick it with a needle; this spreads the infection.

p:aid:0:2.x:
Be especially careful not to squeeze boils around the nose and upper lip, as the infection can spread to the brain.
Do not apply unknown pastes or herbs.
Go to the emergency department if:
A large or very painful boil, or one on the face, spine or between the buttocks.
Fever or shivering, or redness spreading around it.
No improvement within a week, or it keeps coming back.
In people with diabetes or weak immunity.
Recipe: Warm compress for a boil
Bee and wasp stings
Usually treated at home
Do
Remove the sting quickly by scraping it out with the edge of a card or a fingernail.
Wash the area with soap and water.
Apply a cold compress for 10 minutes.
Don't
Do not squeeze the sting with tweezers, as that pushes in the remaining venom.
Do not scratch the area.
Go to the emergency department if:
Emergency now: swelling of the face, lips or tongue, difficulty breathing, wheezing, dizziness, or a rash all over the body (anaphylaxis). If the person has an adrenaline pen, use it at once.
Many stings, or a sting inside the mouth or throat.
Jellyfish sting
Usually treated at home
Do
Get out of the water.
Rinse the area with seawater.
Remove stuck tentacles with tweezers or a glove, not with your bare hand.
Vinegar helps with some species before removing the tentacles.
Soak the area in water as hot as you can tolerate (without burning) for 20–40 minutes; it eases the pain.
Don't
Do not rinse it with fresh tap water, as it may release more venom.
Do not rub the area with sand or a towel.
Do not urinate on it; this is a myth.
Go to the emergency department if:
Difficulty breathing or chest pain.
A sting over a large area, or in a child.
Severe swelling or dizziness.
Mosquito and insect bites
Usually treated at home
Do
Wash the area with soap and water.
Apply a cold compress.
Chilled aloe gel eases the itch (see the recipe).
Trim children's nails to reduce scratching.
Don't
Do not scratch the bite, so it does not get infected.
Go to the emergency department if:
Signs of severe allergy: facial swelling or difficulty breathing.
Spreading redness or pus.
Fever, headache or joint pain after a mosquito bite in affected areas.
Recipe: Aloe gel for insect bites
Burns
Usually treated at home
Do
Cool the burn at once under lukewarm or cool (not iced) running water for a full 20 minutes.
Remove rings and watches before swelling, and clothing that is not stuck.
Cover with clean cling film or a non-fluffy dressing.
For small superficial burns after cooling: aloe gel (see the recipe).
Don't
Do not put ice directly on it.

p:aid:0:3.x:
Do not apply toothpaste, butter, ghee, oil, coffee or egg white.
Do not pop blisters.
Go to the emergency department if:
A burn larger than the palm of the hand, or with large blisters.
Burns to the face, hands, feet, joints or genitals.
Electrical or chemical burns.
A white or charred burn without pain (a deep burn).
Burns in children and older people.
Recipe: Chilled aloe gel
Heatstroke and heat exhaustion
Emergency now
Do
Heatstroke is an emergency: a very high temperature with confusion, fainting or seizures. Call an ambulance immediately.
Move the person into the shade or an air-conditioned place.
Remove extra clothing.
Cool them quickly: cold water on the body, and ice packs on the neck, armpits and upper thighs, with a fan.
If conscious: sips of water or rehydration solution.
Heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, dizziness and cramps): rest in a cool place with fluids, and keep watching.
Don't
Never give water to someone who is unconscious.
Never leave a child in a closed car, even for minutes.
Do not give fever medicines for heatstroke; they do not help.
Go to the emergency department if:
Confusion, slurred speech, fainting or seizures.
Sweating stops, with hot, dry skin.
Repeated vomiting that prevents drinking.
Nosebleed
Usually treated at home
Do
Sit and lean your head slightly forward.
Pinch the soft part of the nose with two fingers for 10–15 minutes without letting go to look.
Breathe through your mouth, and spit out the blood rather than swallowing it.
A cold compress on the bridge of the nose may help.
Don't
Do not tip your head back; it makes blood run into the throat and stomach.
Do not lie on your back.
Do not blow your nose hard for hours after the bleeding stops.
Go to the emergency department if:
Bleeding for more than 20 minutes despite pressure.
After a blow to the head or face.
On blood thinners, or if it happens often.
Sprains and bruises
Usually treated at home
Do
Rest: stop using the injured joint.
Ice: wrapped in cloth, 15–20 minutes every 2–3 hours for the first two days.
Compression: an elastic bandage, not too tight.
Elevation: raise the limb above heart level.
Don't
Do not massage a sprain hard in the first days.
Do not apply heat in the first 48 hours.
Do not go to a folk bone-setter before making sure there is no fracture.
Go to the emergency department if:
Unable to bear weight, or an obvious deformity.
Numbness, coldness or colour change in the limb.
Severe pain that does not improve within two days.
Swallowing a poisonous substance or plant
Emergency now
Do
Call an ambulance or your country's poison centre immediately.

p:aid:0:4.x:
Keep the container or a piece of the plant to identify the substance.
If the substance is on the skin or in the eye: rinse under running water for 15 minutes.
Common dangerous plants include oleander, harmal, bitter almonds, colocynth and castor seeds.
Don't
Do not try to make the person vomit.
Do not give milk, oil or «anti-poison» herbs.
Do not wait for symptoms to appear.
Go to the emergency department if:
Every case of swallowing a poisonous substance or a large amount of medicine, especially in children.

p:folk:0:0.t: Folk customs: what is sound and what harms
p:folk:0:0.x:
Customs we inherited from our mothers and grandmothers with love and care: some are beneficial and some have proved harmful. Here is the origin of each custom, what medicine says, and the safe alternative, out of respect for our heritage and to protect children and mothers.
All
What harms
With care
What is sound
Salting the newborn
Harmful
The custom: The newborn's skin is rubbed with salt or washed in salty water for days, to «strengthen the skin» and reduce sweat and smell, in the Gulf, Yemen and some rural areas.
What medicine says
A newborn's skin is thin and absorbs salt easily. Cases of dangerously high blood salt, dehydration and skin ulcers have been recorded, some needing intensive care.
The safe alternative
Washing the baby with lukewarm water is enough, with a simple moisturiser for dry skin on a doctor's advice.
Kohl for newborns and children
Harmful
The custom: Kohl or ithmid is put in a newborn's eyes to «widen» them or to ward off the evil eye and envy.
What medicine says
Most unlicensed traditional kohl contains lead, absorbed through the eyes, hands and mouth, which harms a child's brain and development. It can also spread eye infections.
The safe alternative
No kohl at all for babies and children. For adults, a licensed kohl that lists its ingredients.
Related pages
Ithmid
Incense for newborns and new mothers
With care
The custom: The newborn, the new mother and the room are perfumed with incense, harmal or frankincense smoke, for a pleasant smell, to ward off the evil eye and to purify the place.
What medicine says
Smoke in a closed room irritates a baby's lungs, increases asthma attacks and chest infections, and can build up carbon monoxide. Harmal is poisonous if eaten or drunk.
The safe alternative
No incense in the baby's room or near the baby. If the house is perfumed, do it away from the child, and open the windows before they return.
Related pages
Harmal
Frankincense
Tahneek with a date
Sound
The custom: A Prophetic Sunnah: a date is chewed and rubbed on the newborn's palate in the first days.
Abu Musa said: «A boy was born to me, so I brought him to the Prophet ﷺ, who named him Ibrahim and did tahneek for him with a date» (Bukhari and Muslim).
What medicine says
A tiny amount of date does no harm. But chewing the date in the mouth can pass the herpes virus to the newborn, which is very dangerous for them. Honey is forbidden for babies because of the risk of botulism.
The safe alternative

p:folk:0:1.t: Folk customs: what is sound and what harms
p:folk:0:1.x:
Mash the date with a clean spoon or soften it with a little water instead of chewing it, and rub a very small amount on the palate. No one with a cold sore (herpes) on their lips should do it.
Related pages
Dates and fresh dates
Ash, coffee and toothpaste on wounds and the umbilical cord
Harmful
The custom: Ash, ground coffee, kohl, toothpaste or oil is put on the newborn's cord, wounds and burns, to stop bleeding or «dry them».
What medicine says
These substances are not sterile and can cause infection, including tetanus, which kills newborns. Toothpaste traps the heat of a burn.
The safe alternative
The cord: keep it clean, dry and open to the air until it falls off by itself. Wounds: wash with clean water and cover with a clean dressing. Burns: lukewarm running water for 20 minutes.
Cautery and branding (kayy and wasm)
Harmful
The custom: The skin is burned with a heated nail or iron to treat jaundice, stomach pain, epilepsy, coughs and more, and it is still practised in some homes.
The Prophet ﷺ said: «Healing is in three things: a cut of the cupping blade, a drink of honey, or cautery with fire, and I forbid my community from cautery» (Bukhari).
What medicine says
It causes deep burns, permanent scars and infections, and delays real treatment of serious illnesses such as newborn jaundice, which can harm the brain.
The safe alternative
A doctor first. Newborn jaundice should be checked the same day, and it is treated with light therapy in hospital.
Folk bonesetters
With care
The custom: Someone with a fracture or sprain is taken to a folk bonesetter, who resets the bone and binds it with splints and cloth.
What medicine says
Some are skilled with simple sprains, but fractures need an X-ray. Binding too tightly can cut off blood to the limb so that the muscle dies, and most victims are children. A fracture that heals crooked may later need surgery.
The safe alternative
An X-ray at the doctor's first for any injury with severe swelling, deformity or inability to move. If a limb has been bound, the danger signs are pain getting worse and cold, blue or numb fingers or toes: undo the binding at once and go to the emergency department.
Pouring lead
Harmful
The custom: Lead is melted over a fire and poured into water above the sick person's head, to reveal or break the evil eye and envy.
What medicine says
Fumes from melted lead are poisonous and are breathed in inside the home, most dangerously by children and pregnant women. It can also cause burns.
The safe alternative
Ruqyah with the Quran and supplications needs no lead or anything else.

p:folk:0:2.t: Folk customs: what is sound and what harms
p:folk:0:2.x:
The postpartum belt (binding the belly)
Sound
The custom: The new mother binds her belly with cloth or a belt after birth to tighten it and support her back.
What medicine says
A comfortable belt does no harm and may ease back pain and give comfort after a caesarean with the doctor's approval. But it does not flatten the belly by itself, and binding too tightly presses on the organs and restricts breathing.
The safe alternative
A comfortable, non-compressing belt, loosened if it feels tight. After a caesarean, only with the doctor's approval. Pelvic floor and tummy exercises after asking the doctor.
The forty days after birth
With care
The custom: The new mother stays at home for forty days, is fed warm foods such as fenugreek, broth and aseeda, is looked after by the family, and is kept very warm.
What medicine says
Rest, family support and nourishing food are among the best things there are and protect against postnatal depression. But staying in bed entirely raises the risk of blood clots in the legs. Overheating in summer causes heat exhaustion. And there is no basis for avoiding bathing or drinking less water.
The safe alternative
Rest with gentle walking around the house from the first days, plenty of water especially while breastfeeding, bathing in warm water, and a room at a moderate temperature. If deep sadness or frightening thoughts appear, see a doctor at once.
Related pages
Fenugreek
Tight swaddling of the newborn
With care
The custom: The newborn is wrapped tightly with the legs straight and pressed together, to calm them and straighten the legs.
What medicine says
Wrapping calms a baby, but holding the legs straight raises the risk of developmental hip dislocation. Over-wrapping in the heat raises the baby's temperature.
The safe alternative
If swaddling, wrap only the upper body, leaving the legs free and bent like a frog's, with light cloth. Always put the baby to sleep on their back.
Water and herbs for babies (gripe water, anise, cumin)
Harmful
The custom: In the first weeks the baby is given water, anise or cumin infusion, or «gripe water» for colic and wind.
What medicine says
A baby under 6 months needs nothing but milk. Water and herbs fill the stomach so the baby feeds and gains less, and too much water can lower blood salt and cause seizures. Star anise can also be mixed up with a Japanese variety that is toxic to the nerves.
The safe alternative
For colic: hold the baby, pat them, massage the tummy gently, and check the feeding technique. From 6 months, water is given with food.
Related pages
Anise
Cumin

p:folk:0:3.t: Folk customs: what is sound and what harms
p:folk:0:3.x:
Henna for newborns and children
With care
The custom: A newborn or child is decorated with henna for occasions or to cool the body.
What medicine says
In children with G6PD deficiency, which is common in the Gulf, henna can cause the blood to break down and severe jaundice. «Black henna» mixed with PPD causes burns and lifelong allergy.
The safe alternative
No henna for newborns. For older children: only after checking the G6PD test, and only natural red henna, never black.
Related pages
Henna
Amber and bead necklaces for teething
Harmful
The custom: The baby wears an amber or bead necklace or bracelet to ease teething pain or ward off the evil eye.
What medicine says
There is no evidence it eases teething, and cases of choking and strangulation by necklaces, and swallowed beads, have been recorded.
The safe alternative
A teething ring chilled in the fridge (not frozen), and rubbing the gums with a clean finger.
Wrapping a feverish person in blankets
Harmful
The custom: The feverish person is wrapped in blankets «to sweat» so that the fever breaks.
What medicine says
Lots of covers raise the temperature further and cause dehydration, and can lead to seizures in children.
The safe alternative
Light clothing, a moderately cool room, plenty of fluids, and a doctor if there are danger signs.
Recipe: Cooling fever with water
If you know a folk custom common in your country that we have not mentioned, send it to us through the «Share your recipe» form in «Mum's recipes».

p:nutri:2:0.t: Food & vitamins — When do you need a test and a doctor?
p:nutri:2:0.x:
Tiredness, paleness or shortness of breath lasting more than two weeks.
Numbness in the limbs or poor memory.
Before and during pregnancy, and with heavy periods.
With long-term medicines such as metformin and acid medicines, or after stomach surgery.
Do not take «vitamin injections» or high doses without a test; too much of some vitamins is as harmful as too little.

p:mind:0:0.x:
Our physicians were early to see sadness, anxiety and obsessions as illnesses treated with gentleness, talk and good order, not a shame to hide. Here is what our heritage holds, what science says today, and what to beware of.
Important: If you or someone you know has thoughts of self-harm or suicide, seek help at once from emergency services, a doctor or someone you trust. Herbs do not replace a psychiatrist, and a prescribed medicine is not stopped because of them.

p:mind:1:0.t: The mind in heritage — Our physicians and the mind
p:mind:1:0.x:
Abu Zayd al-Balkhi
9th century CE
In his book «Sustenance of Bodies and Souls» he discussed fear and anxiety, sadness and depression, and obsessions as conditions to be treated, in a way researchers see as close to today's cognitive behavioural therapy, while also attending to the soul and the worship of God.
Ishaq ibn Imran (Kairouan)
9th century CE
Around 900 CE he wrote «A Treatise on Melancholia», one of the oldest writings on depression; Constantine the African translated it into Latin and it spread in Europe.
Abu Bakr al-Razi
9th–10th century CE
He is considered a pioneer of psychiatry and psychotherapy, and in his book for the general public listed melancholia among the illnesses to be treated just like bodily ones.
Ibn Sina (Avicenna)
11th century CE
In «The Canon» he described «lovesickness» as an illness, with a way to identify the beloved: the physician names people and places while feeling the patient's pulse, and a change in the pulse at a name reveals the beloved. It is one of the oldest examples of the mind's effect on the body.
The bimaristans (hospitals)
9th to 14th century CE
They turned no one away and had separate wards for mental patients. Music was used in their treatment at the Mansuri hospital of Qalawun in Cairo, and the Arghun hospital in Aleppo is said to have relied on light, air and running water. The Nuri hospital in Damascus was the first to keep patient records.

p:mind:2:0.t: The mind in heritage — Herbs for mood and anxiety: in heritage and today
p:mind:2:0.x:
Herb	In heritage	Today
Saffron
Sound	«Exhilarant» that strengthens the heart and lifts sadness	In short studies (up to 8 weeks) on moderate depression, 30 mg a day worked about as well as some antidepressants. Do not exceed this; pregnant women should not take it as a remedy because large amounts stimulate the uterus, and people on blood thinners should be cautious.
Lavender
Sound	«Broom of the brain» that clears it of humours	Studies of a lavender-oil product made for swallowing suggest an effect on anxiety, but they are small and mostly company-funded. Tea or inhaling is generally enough; never drink raw essential oil. It may add to the effect of sedatives.
Chamomile
Sound	Calms the nerves and the stomach	Limited evidence of a modest effect on mild anxiety, and less for sleep. Safe for most people, but it can cause allergy in those sensitive to ragweed, daisies, sunflowers and their plant family.
Lemon balm
Sound	Drives away obsessions and gladdens the heart	Small studies with inconsistent results for anxiety, and little evidence for sleep. No notable harms were recorded in studies, but its safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding is unknown.
Barley
Sound	Talbina takes away some sadness	A warm, comforting food for the sick and the sad, with no evidence that it treats depression.
Valerian
With care	For insomnia and anxiety	Evidence for sleep is inconsistent; the American Academy of Sleep Medicine advises against it for chronic insomnia, and there is not enough evidence for anxiety. Do not take it with sleeping pills or sedatives; rare cases of liver injury have been reported.
Ashwagandha
With care	Tonic and calming in Indian medicine	Studies on stress and sleep, but cases of liver injury, overactive thyroid and adrenal suppression have been reported. Not suitable in pregnancy; the Dutch health institute advises pregnant women to avoid it completely.
St John's wort
With care	For sadness and gloom in Europe	Better than placebo in mild to moderate depression, but not effective in severe depression. It interacts strongly with many medicines: antidepressants (risk of «serotonin syndrome»), birth-control pills, warfarin, digoxin and transplant drugs. Take it only after asking the doctor, and not in pregnancy or breastfeeding.

p:mind:3:0.t: The mind in heritage — The Prophetic talbina
p:mind:3:0.x:
Authentic (sahih) hadithAisha (may God be pleased with her) used to recommend talbina, saying: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: “Talbina gives rest to the heart of the sick and takes away some of the grief” (Bukhari).
Cook two tablespoons of wholegrain barley flour in a cup of milk or water over low heat for 10 minutes, stirring, until it is like a soup.
Sweeten with a spoon of honey once it has cooled a little, and add dates or a little cinnamon.
Eat it warm; it suits the sick, the sad and the convalescent, and is fine from age one, without honey before then.
People with diabetes should watch the honey and dates, and people with coeliac disease avoid barley.

p:mind:4:0.t: The mind in heritage — Habits and practices: what is right and what harms
p:mind:4:0.x:
All
Sound
Harmful
Practice	In heritage	Today
Talking and counsel
Sound	Al-Balkhi treated sadness and fear with comforting talk and changing thoughts.	Talking therapy (psychotherapy) is one of the most successful treatments for anxiety and depression today.
Movement, sunshine and nature
Sound	Exercise, walking and gardens in the physicians' advice.	Exercise, especially walking, running and swimming, eases depression and anxiety with strong evidence, and in some cases its effect approaches that of therapy and medication. Ask the doctor where it fits in treatment.
Regular sleep and food
Sound	«Ordering» sleep and food is the basis of treatment for Ibn Sina.	Regular sleep and balanced food protect against bouts of anxiety and sadness.
Prayer, remembrance of God and ruqya
Sound	Peace of heart through remembrance, the Quran and transmitted supplications.	They comfort the soul and are fine alongside treatment, not instead of it.
Family company, not isolation
Sound	The patient is kept company, not left alone.	Social support is one of the strongest protections against depression.
Stopping the doctor's medicine and replacing it with herbs
Harmful	«Natural is better».	Stopping antidepressants suddenly causes withdrawal symptoms, some of which feel like the illness returning. The dose is reduced gradually over weeks or months with a plan agreed with the doctor.
Cautery
Harmful	The head or body is burned to drive out the illness.	It does nothing for mental illness, and causes burns, infection and pain.
Beating, tying up and locking away
Harmful	On the pretext of driving jinn out of the patient.	Harm and torture of the patient; patients have died from it. Mental illness is an illness to be treated.
Charlatans and amulets
Harmful	Paying money to frauds and hanging up talismans.	They have no basis, delay treatment and drain the family.
Hiding the patient for fear of shame
Harmful	«So people won't know».	Delay makes the illness more severe and harder to treat. Mental illness is like bodily illness, with no shame in it.

p:mind:5:0.x:
What is autism?
A difference in brain development that appears in the early years, affecting communication and interaction with people, with repetitive behaviour and narrow interests. Its degrees vary greatly. It is not caused by upbringing, the evil eye or vaccines.
Signs that call for seeing a doctor
Not turning to their name by age one, not pointing with a finger, little eye contact, delayed speech, repetitive movements, or losing words or skills they had mastered. Losing skills at any age calls for a doctor at once.
What is proven to help
Early diagnosis, then behavioural and educational intervention, speech and language therapy, occupational therapy, parent training, and support for the child at school. The earlier it starts, the better.
Food and sleep
Eating problems, constipation and sleep problems are common in autistic children, and the paediatrician treats them. Do not impose a strict diet without a doctor and a dietitian.
In folk tradition
Autism was not known as a diagnosis in old medicine, so there is no treatment for it in the tradition, and no herb or folk mixture has been proven to treat it.

p:mind:6:0.t: The mind in heritage — Beware of these «treatments»
p:mind:6:0.x:
Harmful
MMS or «chlorine dioxide» solution: the US FDA says drinking it is «the same as drinking bleach»; it has caused serious poisonings and deaths, and the FDA warns never to give it to children for any reason.
«Removing metals» from the body (chelation) without proven poisoning: dangerous; a five-year-old autistic boy died from it in the US in 2005.
Claims that camel milk, honey or some mixture cures autism: camel-milk studies are few, small and only weeks long, and the review that pooled them was retracted. It must not replace treatment.
«Stem cells» sold in unlicensed clinics.
Cautery, beating and locking away, and fraudulent healers who promise a cure for money.
Where to get help: the family doctor or paediatrician first, then a psychiatrist or a child-development assessment centre. Every family with an autistic child has a right to support, and there is no shame in asking for it.

p:eye:0:0.x: Arab eye doctors were called «kahhal», and their books on the eye were among the finest medicine reached before modern times. Here is their history, folk habits that help and harm, the common eye diseases in our region, and emergency signs.

p:eye:1:0.t: The eye in heritage — Go to emergency at once if
p:eye:1:0.x:
Sudden loss of sight, even in one eye.
Severe eye pain and redness with blurred vision.
Strong sensitivity to light with a red eye.
Double vision with a drooping eyelid.
Flashes of light or a «curtain» covering part of the vision.
An eye injury or a foreign body that will not come out.
A chemical in the eye: rinse with running water for 15 minutes first, then go to emergency.

p:eye:2:0.t: The eye in heritage — A journey through the history of eye medicine
p:eye:2:0.x:
Babylon: the Code of Hammurabi
around 1750 BCE
One of the oldest written laws: it set the physician's fee for healing an eye with his lancet, and punished him by cutting off his hand if the patient lost the eye. Eye surgery was known, and dangerous, even then.
Ancient Egypt
around 1550 BCE
The Ebers Papyrus has dozens of remedies for eye diseases. The Egyptians used green kohl (from malachite) and black kohl (from galena) as adornment and protection from sun and flies.
India: Sushruta
Before the Common Era
Couching is attributed to his school: pushing the clouded lens of the eye back inside with a needle. It was common among Indian surgeons and is among the oldest known cataract operations.
Greece and Rome
1st and 2nd centuries CE
Celsus described couching, and Galen wrote on the anatomy of the eye, believing the lens was the seat of sight.
Hunayn ibn Ishaq
9th century CE
He wrote «Ten Treatises on the Eye» in Baghdad, the oldest known systematic book of ophthalmology: the eye's anatomy, diseases and surgery. One of its old copies contains a famous diagram of the eye.
Abu Bakr al-Razi
9th–10th century CE
One of the first to describe the pupil narrowing in light and widening in the dark, in his book «al-Hawi».
Ammar ibn Ali al-Mawsili
5th century AH / 11th century CE (Egypt)
He settled in Egypt under the caliph al-Hakim and wrote for him «The Book of Choice in Ophthalmology». In it he described a hollow needle he made and used to remove a cataract from the eye, an idea close to cataract surgery today.
Ali ibn Isa al-Kahhal
11th century CE
He wrote «Memorandum for Eye Doctors», describing more than a hundred eye diseases and their treatment. In Europe he was known as «Jesu Occulist», and its physicians used his book for centuries.
Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen)
11th century CE
In his «Book of Optics» he proved that sight happens when light enters the eye, not by a ray leaving it as the Greeks thought, basing this on experiment. His book influenced optics scholars in Europe.
Khalifa ibn Abi al-Mahasin of Aleppo
13th century CE
He wrote «The Sufficient Book on Ophthalmology» (died 1256), arranging eye-surgery instruments in tables, each with its drawing, name and use. He also described using a magnet to pull a broken piece of a couching needle out of the eye.
Ibn al-Nafis
13th century CE
He wrote «The Refined Book of Tested Ophthalmology» in Cairo, gathering what he had tried in treating the eye.
Salah al-Din al-Kahhal of Hama
around 1296 CE
He lived in Hama and wrote for his son «Light of the Eyes», a detailed book on ophthalmology.
Words that remain
Until today

p:eye:2:1.t: The eye in heritage — A journey through the history of eye medicine
p:eye:2:1.x: It is said that the Latin names of the layers of the eye, such as retina and cornea, translate the Arabic names in the eye doctors' books, and that the cataract was named as a translation of «water descending in the eye».

p:eye:3:0.t: The eye in heritage — Folk habits: what is right and what harms
p:eye:3:0.x:
All
Sound
With care
Harmful
Habit	In heritage	Today
Clean warm compress
Sound	Compresses are among the eye doctors' oldest treatments.	For a stye and inflamed eyelid edges: about 5 minutes, two to four times a day, with gentle eyelid massage. Do not leave heat on the eye for long.
Cold compress
Sound	Cooling an inflamed eye.	Eases allergy itching and swollen eyelids.
Rinsing the eye with clean running water
Sound	Washing out what got into the eye.	The most important step when dust or a chemical gets in: 15 minutes of running water, then the doctor.
Protecting the eyes from sun and dust
Sound	Turbans, face veils and the shade of tents.	Sunglasses in the Gulf protect against pterygium and cataract.
Chamomile or tea compresses
With care	Tea bags on tired eyes.	Only on closed eyelids, with boiled, cooled, clean water. They can cause allergy and are no better than a plain compress.
Drops of lemon, onion or garlic juice or home-made herbal drops
Harmful	«They clean the eye and strengthen sight».	They burn the cornea and can carry germs and fungi that cause ulcers and loss of sight.
Breast milk or urine in the eye
Harmful	To treat conjunctivitis and a baby's inflamed eye.	Neither its safety nor its benefit is proven, and it can delay proper treatment. An inflamed eye in a newborn can cause blindness, so a doctor should see it at once.
Raw truffle juice in the eye
Harmful	Understanding the hadith «and its water is a cure for the eye» literally.	Truffles come from the ground and carry germs and fungi. Scholars understood the hadith in several ways, and it does not mean dropping it directly into the eye.
Unlicensed traditional kohl
Harmful	Applying kohl is Sunnah, and newborns are given kohl.	Much of it contains toxic lead, sometimes more than half its weight, which is especially dangerous for children. Choose licensed lead-free kohl, and do not put kohl on a newborn.
Folk couching of cataract
Harmful	Pushing the lens back with a needle by unqualified people.	Its results for sight are usually poor, as Nigeria's national blindness survey found. Cataract surgery today is safe and quick.
Cautery around the eye
Harmful	To treat conjunctivitis or weak sight.	It does not help and causes burns and eyelid deformity.

p:eye:4:0.t: The eye in heritage — Herbs and foods for the eye: in heritage and today
p:eye:4:0.x:
Item	In heritage	Today
Fennel	«Fennel sharpens the sight» in Arab books, and Pliny reported that snakes rub their eyes on it.	No evidence that it strengthens sight. Eat it as food, and never put it in the eye.
Eggs	Food of strength.	The yolk is rich in lutein, zeaxanthin and vitamin A, which benefit the retina.
Goji berry	Strengthens sight in Chinese medicine.	Rich in zeaxanthin, a pigment that concentrates in the retina, but no studies show it protects the retina. One case of bleeding with warfarin has been reported.
Saffron	Clears the sight, according to some old physicians.	Small trials on macular degeneration (a retinal disease of older age); results are preliminary.
Ithmid	«It clears the sight and makes the hair grow».	Choose only licensed, lead-free kohl.
Desert truffle	«And its water is a cure for the eye».	Eat it cooked, and never put its juice in the eye.
For the eyes in general: dark leafy greens such as spinach and rocket, carrots and sweet potato, fish twice a week, and no smoking.

p:eye:5:0.t: The eye in heritage — Common eye diseases in our region
p:eye:5:0.x:
Diabetes and the retina
One of the commonest complications of diabetes, and it can lead to blindness. In a UAE study many patients did not know their eyes were affected. So every diabetic needs a yearly eye exam, and good control of sugar and blood pressure.
Cataract
Clouding of the lens that comes with age, sun and diabetes. It is treated with quick, safe surgery; folk drops do not remove it.
Glaucoma
It silently damages the eye's nerve. The American Academy of Ophthalmology advises a full eye exam by age forty at the latest, and people with a family history are four to nine times more likely to get it.
Pterygium
A fleshy growth on the white of the eye, mainly caused by ultraviolet light, then dust, sand and wind. Prevention: sunglasses that block UV light, and a brimmed hat.
Dry eye
From air conditioning, screens and wind, because we blink less at screens. It is eased by full blinking, the 20-20-20 rule (every 20 minutes look at something far away for 20 seconds), and keeping air-conditioner airflow off the face. If it lasts 3–4 weeks, see an eye doctor.
Conjunctivitis (pink eye)
Redness and discharge, mostly contagious. Wash hands, do not share towels, and see a doctor if sight weakens or pain grows.
Squint and lazy eye in children
Treatment works best before age seven; older children can still improve, but less. An eye test before school is essential.
No herb or folk drop treats cataract, glaucoma or retinal disease. The eye doctor is the reference, and regular check-ups protect sight.

p:safety:6:0.t: Safety checker — Look-alike and poisonous plants
p:safety:6:0.x:
Compare for yourself: each plant has a link to real photos from the free Wikimedia library.
Poison hemlock and the parsley family
Parsley Photos ↗ · Anise Photos ↗ · Fennel Photos ↗
⚠ Poison hemlock Photos ↗
Poison hemlock is a wild, poisonous plant of the same family as parsley, carrot, fennel and anise, and looks like them with its finely divided leaves and umbrella-shaped clusters of white flowers. Its stem is smooth and hairless, with red or purple spots, and it can grow to two metres. Poisonings have occurred in people who mistook it for wild parsley. Don't pick plants of this family from the wild, buy your herbs from a known source, and wear gloves if you touch it.
Star anise: Chinese and Japanese
Chinese star anise Photos ↗
⚠ Japanese star anise Photos ↗
The Chinese kind is a safe spice, but the Japanese kind is toxic and used only for decoration, and the two cannot be told apart by eye once dried. In 2003 the US Food and Drug Administration warned against star anise tea after about 40 poisonings, 15 of them infants, with seizures and vomiting. Never give star anise tea to a baby for colic. It is different from ordinary anise, the small seeds in this guide.
Desert truffles and wild mushrooms
Desert truffle Photos ↗
⚠ Amanita mushrooms Photos ↗
Desert truffles (fagaa) grow underground and are dug up. White mushrooms that appear above ground after rain may be Amanita, most of which are poisonous, and Kuwait's Environment Public Authority has warned against them. Don't eat a wild mushroom that grew above ground.

p:safety:7:0.t: Safety checker — Wild poisonous plants around us
p:safety:7:0.x:
Oleander
Nerium oleander Photos ↗
A common ornamental in streets and gardens. All parts are poisonous, especially the leaves, and it affects the heartbeat. If any part is swallowed: emergency department immediately.
Colocynth
Citrullus colocynthis Photos ↗
Grows in the desert. The Abu Dhabi Department of Health says all its parts are unsafe and can kill even in small amounts.
Thorn apple (Datura)
Datura stramonium Photos ↗
Grows wild in many parts of Saudi Arabia. Eating its seeds causes agitation, hallucinations and dilated pupils, and children are more affected.
Harmal
Peganum harmala Photos ↗
Burned as incense, but its seeds are toxic to the nerves and heart: they cause hallucinations, tremor, vomiting and low blood pressure, and can cause miscarriage.
If someone swallows an unknown plant: don't wait for symptoms. Call an ambulance or go to the emergency department, and take a piece of the plant or a photo of it with you.
Dangerous herbs we recommend for no one (15)

Colocynth (handhal) — Causes bloody diarrhoea, severe colitis and dehydration that can be fatal
Oleander (difla) — A single leaf can be fatal to children

p:organic:0:0.x:
Grow your herbs and vegetables clean, without pesticides or chemical fertilisers, using methods suited to the heat of our Arab lands, with special care for the Gulf's sandy soil and salty water. For homes and beds first, with tips for those with a farm, and a planting calendar for each Arab region.
Improving sandy soil
Making compost at home
Natural pest control
Watering and saving water in the heat
Companion planting
Saving local seeds
For farmers: organic certification and marketing
Planting calendar
From Andalusian heritage
Farming books through history
Pest prevention in heritage
Beneficial microbes EM
Easy herbs to grow
Improving sandy soil
UAE soil is mostly sandy, poor in organic matter and tends to be alkaline and salty, so it holds neither water nor nutrients. The basis of organic farming is feeding the soil, not the plant.
Related herbs
Fenugreek
Do
Add a 5–10 cm layer of compost and mix it into the top 20–30 cm of soil before each season.
At home: raised beds or pots filled with a mix of sand, compost and coconut fibre (cocopeat).
Grow legumes such as clover and broad beans in winter, then turn them into the soil before they flower to enrich it with nitrogen (green manure).
Always cover the soil surface with straw, dry leaves or shredded palm fronds; bare soil bakes in the sun.
Find out the salinity of your irrigation water and soil with a simple test; salt is the biggest enemy of farming in the Gulf.
Avoid
Fresh animal manure: it burns roots and can carry dangerous germs and weed seeds. Use it only after composting it for at least two to three months.
Chemical fertilisers and synthetic pesticides: not used in organic farming.
Tilling the soil and leaving it bare in summer.
If you have a farm
Before the season: have your soil and water tested by an accredited lab, and record the amounts of organic fertiliser you add each season; this will help with organic certification later.
Making compost at home
Compost is an organic fertiliser you make yourself from kitchen and garden waste, and it is the best thing to add to sandy soil. Our heat speeds up decomposition, as long as the pile does not dry out.
Do
Collect dry «brown» materials: dead leaves, shredded palm fronds, cardboard without glossy ink, and untreated sawdust.
And collect moist «green» materials: vegetable and fruit scraps, coffee grounds and tea leaves, and grass clippings.
Mix roughly two to three parts brown to one part green, in a bin with holes or a heap in the shade.
Keep it as damp as a wrung-out sponge: in summer sprinkle it with water every two to three days, and cover it.

p:organic:0:1.x:
Turn it once a week. It is ready in two to three months, when it is dark and smells like earth after rain.
Worm compost: special red worms in a box indoors, because summer heat above 35° kills them.
Avoid
Meat, fish, dairy and oils: they attract insects and cats and cause bad smells.
Cat and dog droppings, and diseased plants.
Letting the heap dry out completely in the sun, which stops decomposition.
If you have a farm
On a farm: make long compost rows and turn them by machine, and mix livestock manure with shredded palm waste; a single palm gives large amounts of fronds each year.
Natural pest control
Prevention first: a strong plant in rich soil, grown in its proper season, resists pests better. If a pest appears, start with the gentlest option.
Related herbs
Neem
Garlic
Dill
Coriander
Do
Check the undersides of leaves every week, and remove affected leaves early.
A strong jet of water knocks aphids off the leaves.
Potassium soap made for gardening, for aphids and whitefly, as directed on the pack.
Neem oil made for gardening, as directed on the pack.
A garlic and hot chilli infusion repels some insects; strain it well and test it on one leaf first.
Yellow sticky traps for whitefly and flying insects.
Beneficial bacteria (Bt) for caterpillars that eat the leaves; allowed in organic farming, as directed on the pack.
Encourage beneficial insects such as ladybirds by growing dill, coriander and fennel and letting them flower.
Red palm weevil: report it to the municipality or agricultural authority at once; they have control programmes and special traps.
Avoid
Spraying at midday: it burns the leaves. Spray in the evening.
Spraying on flowers while bees are active.
Tobacco infusion: nicotine is toxic to people and animals, and should not be used.
Assuming «natural» means safe: wear gloves, keep children away, and follow the pack instructions and the waiting time before harvest.
Lots of household washing-up liquid: it can burn plants.
If you have a farm
On a farm: record every product you spray and the date; organic certifiers ask for this record and accept only substances permitted under organic standards.
Watering and saving water in the heat
Water is the most precious thing in Gulf farming. Smart watering saves half the water or more and makes plants stronger.
Related herbs
Moringa
Do
Drip irrigation with a timer: it takes water straight to the roots.
Water early in the morning before eight, or after sunset.
Cover the soil with a 5–10 cm layer of straw, leaves or shredded fronds, which greatly reduces the need for watering.

p:organic:0:2.x:
In summer: a 30–50% shade net over vegetables and tender herbs.
Group plants by their water needs: thirsty ones together, drought-tolerant ones together.
Trees get deep, infrequent watering, not a little every day, so their roots grow deep.
Avoid
Watering at midday: most of it evaporates.
Spraying leaves with water in the sun.
Standing water: it rots roots, and moringa and thyme die from it.
Watering leafy vegetables with greywater (from washing and bathing).
If you have a farm
On a farm: check the salinity of well water every season. Salty water needs regular flushing of the soil with heavy watering, and salt-tolerant crops such as palms, sidr and beetroot.
Companion planting
Some plants help each other when grown side by side: they attract beneficial insects, repel harmful ones, or feed the soil. Most of this comes from farmers' experience, with few scientific trials.
Related herbs
Basil
Mint
Fennel
Do
Basil next to tomatoes: an old farmers' habit.
French marigold among vegetables: it attracts pollinators, and its roots may reduce nematodes in the soil.
Legumes such as green beans and broad beans among vegetables: they feed the soil with nitrogen.
Dill, coriander and fennel in flower: they attract ladybirds and beneficial insects.
Onions and garlic around the edges of beds: their smell repels some insects.
Avoid
Mint planted straight in the ground: it spreads and takes over the bed; grow it in a pot.
Fennel next to most vegetables: farmers find it weakens their growth; grow it on its own.
Growing the same crop in the same spot every season: rotate it to reduce disease.
Saving local seeds
Local heirloom seeds have adapted to our heat and soil over generations. Saving them from season to season saves money and preserves varieties that could be lost.
Do
Choose local or «open-pollinated» seeds; hybrid seeds (marked F1) do not give the same plant if their seeds are sown.
Choose the strongest plants with the best fruit, and leave them until their seeds are fully ripe.
Dry the seeds well in the shade for several days.
Store them in a paper envelope or an airtight glass jar in a cool, dry place; the fridge is fine if the jar is airtight.
Write the name and date on each envelope; most seeds stay viable for two to five years.
Swap seeds with neighbours and farmers.
Avoid
Taking seeds from a diseased plant.
Storing them in plastic bags before they are completely dry: they go mouldy.
Leaving them somewhere hot, such as a car or an unair-conditioned store.
For farmers: organic certification and marketing

p:organic:0:3.x:
In the UAE, «organic» may only be written on a product with certification from an accredited body. Organic farming is overseen by the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment, and some emirates have programmes to support farmers, such as Sharjah's programme for converting to organic farming.
Do
Contact the Ministry of Climate Change and Environment or your emirate's agricultural authority to find accredited bodies and support programmes.
Expect a conversion period: the farm follows organic standards for a time before it may sell its produce as «organic».
Keep full records: seeds, fertilisers, spraying, harvests and sales.
Certification also covers packing and storage, so if you dry or pack produce, ask about certifying the factory.
Avoid
Writing «organic» or «100% natural organic» on an uncertified product: a legal violation.
Mixing organic and non-organic produce in storage or packing.

p:organic:2:0.t: Organic farming — From the heritage of Arab and Andalusian farming
p:organic:2:0.x: Between the 10th and 14th centuries, scholars of al-Andalus and Iraq wrote the greatest farming encyclopaedias of their age, in Córdoba, Toledo, Seville and Granada. Their farming was organic by nature: composted manure, careful irrigation, and pest control with ash and herbs.

p:organic:3:0.t: Organic farming — Farming scholars and their books
p:organic:3:0.x:
Ibn Wahshiyya
Iraq, around 904 CE · «Nabataean Agriculture»
The oldest large agricultural encyclopaedia in Arabic, recording the knowledge of the ancient people of Iraq on soil, water and trees. The Andalusians relied on it heavily; alongside the science it contains magical recipes that are not to be followed.
Arib ibn Sa'd and Rabi' ibn Zayd
Córdoba, 961 CE · «The Calendar of Córdoba»
A monthly calendar listing for each month what to sow, plant and harvest, the weather, and when livestock give birth. It is the oldest Andalusian farming calendar to survive.
Ibn Wafid
Toledo, 11th century · «Compendium of Agriculture»
A physician and botanist credited with overseeing al-Ma'mun's royal garden in Toledo, which served as an experimental field for plants.
Ibn Bassal
Toledo, then Seville, 11th century · «The Book of Purpose and Explanation»
A scholar-farmer who based his book on his own hands-on experiments. He divided soil into ten types by colour, texture and fertility, and detailed manures: which suits which plant, and which does harm. He also oversaw the Sultan's garden in Seville.
Abu al-Khayr al-Ishbili
Seville, 11th–12th centuries · «The Physician's Support in Knowing Plants» and «Book of Agriculture»
He described plants precisely: their forms, habitats, seasons, varieties and uses. His book is considered the most extensive Andalusian work of botany.
Al-Tighnari
Granada, early 12th century · «The Flower of the Garden and Delight of Minds»
An agronomist at the court of Granada who wrote on soil, irrigation, grafting and growing cereals and pulses.
Ibn al-Awwam
Seville, late 12th century · «Book of Agriculture»
The most famous farming encyclopaedia of the Middle Ages: it describes growing about 585 plants and more than fifty fruit trees, combining Nabataean, Roman and Andalusian farming with his own experience, and was translated into Spanish and French.
Ibn Luyun al-Tujibi
Almería, 1282–1349 CE · «Exposition of Beauty and Utmost Excellence in the Principles of the Art of Agriculture»
He set the science of agriculture into a long poem in 1348 so farmers could memorise it, and classified plants by use, including ornamental plants and plants for delight.

p:organic:4:0.t: Organic farming — Their methods and what science says today
p:organic:4:0.x:
Method	In the farming books	Today
Soil classification
Sound	Ibn Bassal divided it into ten types, each with the crops and manure that suit it.	Soil science still classifies soil by texture and fertility and chooses crops accordingly.
Composted manure
Sound	They advised composting manure mixed with straw and ash before use, and choosing manure to suit the plant, such as pigeon droppings for weak plants.	It is exactly today's compost, and composting kills germs and weed seeds.
Irrigation and water sharing
Sound	Channels, water wheels, cisterns and underground canals, with water shared among farmers in turns.	The basis of modern irrigation, and the aflaj and Valencia's Water Tribunal still work today.
Grafting
With care	They wrote many methods of grafting trees to improve fruit.	Correct between closely related varieties, but grafting trees from distant families, as some books describe, does not work.
Pest control
Sound	Ash, smoke, infusions of bitter herbs, and olive oil on trunks.	Close to organic pest control today, testing each method on a small area first.
Storing grain and seeds
Sound	Storage in dry granaries and underground pits, with ash or insect-repelling leaves.	A sound principle: dryness and keeping insects away are the basis of seed storage.
Seasons and star lore (anwa')
With care	They tied farming to the seasons of rain and heat and to the rising of stars.	Knowing the seasons is correct and useful, but planting by lunar mansions and horoscopes has no evidence.
Strange recipes
Harmful	Some books contain magical recipes, such as hanging objects on trees to ward off cold or pests.	They have no scientific basis and are not used.

p:organic:5:0.x:
Many crops spread in al-Andalus and Sicily, and their Arabic names survive in Spanish today. Historians differ on how many of them were new and how many were known before.

p:organic:6:0.x:
The Water Tribunal of Valencia
It meets every Thursday outside Valencia Cathedral, as it has for centuries, to settle farmers' irrigation disputes orally, and many historians trace its origin to the Andalusian period. UNESCO added it to the intangible heritage list in 2009.
The aflaj of Oman and Al Ain
Underground and surface channels that carry water by gravity from the mountains to the farms, with water shared among farmers in turns and hours. The aflaj of Oman have been on the World Heritage List since 2006, and the Cultural Sites of Al Ain with their oases since 2011.
The Generalife in Granada
The garden of the Alhambra, with its beds, channels and fountains, is a living witness to the Andalusian art of gardening, and is on the World Heritage List with the Alhambra.

p:organic:7:0.t: Organic farming — Lessons for today's organic farmer
p:organic:7:0.x:
Feed the soil with composted manure; it is where Andalusian scholars began their books: soil, then water, then manure.
Know your soil before you plant, as Ibn Bassal did.
Share water fairly and wisely, for water is the most precious thing in farming.
Experiment with your own hands and keep records, as Ibn Bassal and Ibn al-Awwam wrote down what they had tried.
Take from heritage what agrees with experience and science, and leave what was magic or superstition.
Andalusian medicine recipes in the guide

p:organic:8:0.t: Organic farming — Preventing plant diseases and pests in heritage
p:organic:8:0.x: Thousands of years before chemical pesticides, farmers protected their crops with cleanliness, seasons, ash, sulphur and natural enemies. Many of their methods are now the basis of organic and integrated pest management.

p:organic:9:0.t: Organic farming — A journey through history
p:organic:9:0.x:
Sumer (Iraq)
around 2500 BCE
One of the oldest records in history: sulphur compounds used against insects and mites.
Ancient Egypt
Thousands of years
Grain stored in dry, sealed silos, and cats kept in homes and stores to protect the harvest from mice.
Greece
around 300 BCE
Theophrastus described plant diseases such as rust and blight, and noted that they are worse in damp low-lying places and that some varieties are hardier than others. He was among the first to write about plant diseases.
The Romans
1st century CE
They used amurca (the bitter water left from pressing olives) to repel ants and insects and protect seeds; Cato and Pliny wrote about it.
China
around 304 CE
The first documented biological control: people sold nests of predatory ants to citrus growers and joined the trees with bamboo bridges so the ants would eat the harmful insects.
Iraq: Ibn Wahshiyya
around 904 CE
«The Nabataean Agriculture» has long chapters on pests of trees and crops and their remedies, mixing tested knowledge with magic.
Al-Andalus: Ibn Bassal and Ibn al-Awwam
11th and 12th centuries
Ibn al-Awwam devoted chapters to tree diseases and pests: cleanliness, cutting out what is affected, ash, smoke, herbal infusions, and choosing the right place and time.
The Gulf and Oman
Inherited tradition
Cleaning the palm of old frond bases and dry fibre, covering the date bunches, dusting the palms with sulphur against «ghubair» mites, and sharing aflaj water in a way that stops it standing.

p:organic:10:0.t: Organic farming — Traditional methods and what science says today
p:organic:10:0.x:
All
Sound
With care
Harmful
Method	In heritage	Today
Cleanliness and burning what is diseased
Sound	Cutting out diseased branches and burning them away from the orchard, and removing weeds.	The most important rule of plant protection today: what is infected remains a source of infection.
Collecting fallen fruit
Sound	Gathering and destroying fallen fruit.	It breaks the cycle of fruit flies and worms that live in fallen fruit.
Crop rotation
Sound	Not growing the same crop in the same place every year.	It breaks the cycle of pests and diseases that live in the soil.
Leaving land fallow
With care	The land is left unsown for a year to rest.	Useful, but today it is better to sow legumes as green manure rather than leave it bare.
Choosing seeds and varieties
Sound	Choosing the strongest, healthiest seeds and varieties known to resist disease.	The basis of modern farming: resistant varieties are the cheapest protection.
Timing and site
Sound	Sowing in season, and avoiding damp low-lying places.	Correct: damp and poor air flow are among the main causes of fungal disease.
Pruning for air flow
Sound	Thinning crowded branches.	It lets in air and sun, so fungi and scale insects decrease.
Ash
With care	Scattered on plants, and mixed with stored grain against weevils.	Useful in storage and against snails, but it is alkaline, so do not overuse it on Gulf soil, which is alkaline already.
Sulphur
With care	Dusted as a powder on plants.	Allowed in organic farming against powdery mildew and mites, but it burns leaves in heat above about 32°, so use it early in the morning or in winter.
Amurca (olive-oil lees)
With care	Sprayed to repel ants and insects.	It has a repellent effect, but too much harms the soil and its beneficial organisms.
Smoke
With care	Burning materials in the orchard so the smoke drives insects away.	Its effect is limited and short-lived, and smoke harms people, so it should not be relied on.
Natural enemies
Sound	Predatory ants in China, birds, and chickens under the trees.	Biological control is the basis of organic farming today. But in our gardens ants often protect aphids rather than eat them.
Grafting onto strong rootstocks
Sound	Grafting a good variety onto a strong tree.	Used today to resist soil diseases, drought and salinity.
Covering bunches and fruit
Sound	Bags or nets around date bunches and some fruit.	Effective protection from birds, insects and dust, and it reduces the need for spraying.
Colocynth, oleander and tobacco infusions
Harmful	Sprayed on trees to kill insects.	Poisonous to people, animals and bees, and not used.
Salt around trees

p:organic:10:1.t: Organic farming — Traditional methods and what science says today
p:organic:10:1.x:
Harmful	Scattered to repel termites.	It kills the soil and harms roots, and our soil is salty already.
Frightening a barren tree
Harmful	Striking a tree or threatening it with an axe so it will bear fruit, as some old books describe.	A superstition. Poor fruiting is caused by feeding, watering, pollination or age.
Charms and hanging objects
Harmful	Hanging objects on trees to ward off pests and cold.	They have no basis.

p:organic:11:0.t: Organic farming — What modern science adds for the organic farmer
p:organic:11:0.x:
Soil solarisation at the end of summer: water, then a clear cover for 4–6 weeks.
Pheromone traps for the palm weevil and stem borers, and yellow sticky traps for whitefly.
Spraying white clay (kaolin) on trees: it protects fruit from sunburn and repels some insects, which is very useful in the Gulf heat.
Beneficial bacteria (Bt) for caterpillars, and potassium soap and neem oil for sap-sucking insects.
Copper compounds permitted in organic farming for some fungal diseases, in limited amounts because they build up in the soil.
Plant quarantine: do not move palm offshoots, seedlings or soil from an infested farm, and follow your country's agricultural regulations.

p:organic:12:0.t: Organic farming — Fig pests and prevention
p:organic:12:0.x:
Fruit fly
Collect fallen and damaged fruit daily, pick fruit as soon as it ripens, and hang fruit fly lure traps.
Scale insects and mealybugs
Prune to open up the tree, rub the affected branches, and spray potassium soap or a light horticultural oil in winter when the tree is bare.
Fig rust
Yellow-brown spots on the leaves in humid weather at the end of summer. Gather and destroy fallen leaves, prune for air flow, and do not wet the leaves when watering.
Fig stem borer
Holes in the trunk and sawdust at its base. Cut out and destroy affected branches, seal the holes, and consult the agricultural authority if it spreads.
Fruit rot and beetles
Fruit that splits after heavy watering attracts beetles and rot. Water steadily as the fruit ripens, and pick as you go.
Caprification
Hanging wild figs on the tree for pollination. Only certain varieties need it; most varieties grown in the Gulf fruit without it.

p:organic:13:0.t: Organic farming — Palm pests and prevention
p:organic:13:0.x:
Red palm weevil
The most dangerous palm pest: holes in the trunk, brown ooze and a fermented smell, and a wilting heart. Do not move offshoots from an infested farm, cover pruning wounds, and report it to the agricultural authority at once; they have pheromone traps and control programmes.
Ghubair (dust mite)
Webbing and dust on the bunches that make dates dry and dusty. Cover the bunches, spray water, and dust with sulphur early in the morning, as our grandfathers did.
Dubas bug
An insect that secretes sticky honeydew on the fronds, in Oman, Iraq and the Gulf. Reduce planting density, remove offshoots and weeds around the palm, and control it with the agricultural authority's guidance.
Lesser date moth (humaira)
Small, red, hollow fruits fall early. Collect and destroy fallen fruit, and cover the bunches early.
Cleaning the palm (takreeb)
Removing old frond bases, fibre and dry fronds, which shelter insects and rodents. Do it at the right time, and cover large wounds.
This is general information. If a serious or widespread pest appears, consult your country's agricultural authority, which offers control programmes and free advice to farmers.

p:organic:14:0.t: Organic farming — Beneficial microbes EM and how to activate them
p:organic:14:0.x: EM stands for Effective Microorganisms, developed by the Japanese professor Teruo Higa at the University of the Ryukyus in Okinawa in the 1980s. It is a mix of lactic acid bacteria, photosynthetic bacteria and yeasts in a molasses liquid, sold as EM‑1. Once activated it is called activated solution (EMAS).

p:organic:15:0.t: Organic farming — How to activate it, step by step
p:organic:15:0.x:
1. Quantities
one part original EM‑1, one part molasses (unsulphured sugar-cane molasses) and 18 parts water. Example: one litre of EM‑1, one litre of molasses and 18 litres of water.
2. Water
Chlorine-free water: well water, or tap water left uncovered for a full day so the chlorine escapes. Warm it to about 40° and dissolve the molasses in it first.
3. Container
A clean plastic container (not metal), filled almost to the brim to leave little air, and tightly closed.
4. Fermentation
7 to 10 days in the shade at about 20° to 37°. Open the lid slightly every day in the first days to let gas out, then close it.
5. Sign of success
A pleasant sweet-sour smell like pickles, an orange-brown colour, and a pH between 3.2 and 3.8 on a pH strip. A foul or rotten smell means the solution has spoiled, so do not use it.
6. Storage
In the shade away from sun and heat; use within 30 to 45 days. Do not activate the activated solution a second time; always start from original EM‑1.

p:organic:16:0.t: Organic farming — Uses and what studies say
p:organic:16:0.x:
Use	Method	Evidence
Spraying livestock and poultry barns
Sound	Dilute 1 to 50 or 1 to 100 and spray lightly on the litter, floors and walls, not on the animals or their feed.	A Thai study on broiler chickens: ammonia fell clearly and the birds' stress indicator dropped. It does not replace cleanliness, ventilation and vaccination.
Bokashi (fermenting kitchen scraps)
Sound	Bran moistened with EM solution and molasses is sprinkled in layers over food scraps in a sealed bucket; after two weeks it is buried in the soil.	A tried and successful way to turn kitchen scraps into fertiliser without a foul smell.
Speeding up compost
Sound	Spray the solution diluted 1 to 100 on each layer of the compost heap.	It reduces flies and smell. Its effect on speed and compost quality varies between studies.
With irrigation water for the soil
With care	Dilute 1 to 500 or 1 to 1000 in irrigation water, preferably together with compost, not instead of it.	Results are mixed: most vegetable studies found a positive effect, but the most careful trial (Switzerland) attributed the effect to the molasses and nutrients, not the bacteria.
Fish fertiliser
Sound	Fish fermented with molasses and EM, diluted for spraying or irrigation (method in detail below).	Fish fertiliser itself is a well-known organic fertiliser rich in nitrogen and amino acids, with a proven role in feeding plants.
Spraying plant leaves
With care	Dilute 1 to 500 and spray early in the morning or in the evening.	There is no settled evidence that it prevents disease on its own.
Mud balls in ponds and lakes
Harmful	Balls of clay and bran soaked in the solution and thrown into the water.	Controlled studies (Netherlands 2010, Hawaii 2025) found no improvement; phosphate rose and oxygen fell. Do not throw them into fish ponds or irrigation tanks.
From the site owner's experience (organic farmer): I spray the livestock and poultry barns with the activated solution, and no smells remain. Fish fertiliser fermented with EM is the most successful fertiliser I use on the farm.

p:organic:17:0.t: Organic farming — Fish fertiliser fermented with EM
p:organic:17:0.x:
Fish is rich in nitrogen, amino acids, phosphorus and trace elements, and fish fertiliser is one of the oldest and most successful organic fertilisers. Fermenting it with EM and molasses turns it into an easily absorbed liquid and reduces its smell.
1. Quantities (20-litre drum)
5 kg of fresh fish or fish scraps (heads, guts and bones), 2 litres of molasses, 100 ml of original EM‑1 and 3 litres of chlorine-free water. Instead of the EM‑1 and water, you can use 3 litres of activated solution.
2. Preparation
Cut the fish into small pieces. Dissolve the molasses in warm water and add the EM, then pour it over the fish in a plastic drum and stir well. The fish must be fresh, not rotten.
3. Fermentation
Close the drum tightly and leave it in the shade for two to 3 weeks; it may take a month or more for the fish to dissolve. When the lid swells, open it slightly to let the gas out, then close it.
4. Sign of success
The fish dissolves into a brown liquid with a sour fermented smell. A strong rotten smell like carrion means fermentation failed, usually from too little molasses or air getting in.
5. Straining and storage
Strain through cloth and add the solids to the compost. Bottle it leaving space at the top, and open the caps now and then to let gas out.
6. Use
On leaves: about 150 ml in 16 litres of water (roughly 1 to 100), weekly, early morning or evening. For soil with irrigation water: one litre in 200 litres of water.
7. Note
Do not spray it on leafy vegetables eaten raw close to harvest; stop at least two weeks before picking. Keep it away from children and animals.

p:organic:18:0.t: Organic farming — EM‑5 mix for preventive spraying
p:organic:18:0.x:
One part EM‑1, one part molasses, one part vinegar (white or apple cider), one part distilled alcohol, and 20 parts warm water.
Optionally add crushed garlic, hot pepper, mint or neem.
Close and ferment until the pH falls below 4; it is best left a month before use.
Dilute 1 to 500 and spray on plants weekly, alternating with activated EM‑1.
Do not spray the type containing hot pepper in barns, as it irritates the eyes and breathing of birds and livestock.
EM is a safe product generally accepted in organic farming; its clearest benefits are reducing smells and fermenting compost. It does not replace compost, cleanliness and ventilation.
